3efb9866c2ec5abe: **Aggrega activity-bar view** — four panels in reading order: **Commands**, **Registries**, **Catalog** and **Plugins**. The other three list what your configuration and the workspace hold, and each opens with the operations acting on what it lists, as labelled rows at the head of its list; every other operation is a labelled button on the Commands panel, so each operation has one place to look for it. An operation acting on one particular registry, entity or plugin is on that row. The Commands panel is headed by three single-line rows naming what the editor is acting on — **Project folder**, then **Aggrega workspace**, then **Release** — each opening its own picker. The middle row draws its name shortened, as **Agg. worksp.**, so that each row's value has more of the panel's width; its hover names it in full, as **Aggrega workspace**, and so does every message about it. Their values stand in one column, after the widest of the three labels; in a panel too narrow for that label, it is cut short with an ellipsis rather than pushing the panel sideways, and the row's hover still says which it is. They are in that order because each sits inside the one above it, and the arrangement is how that is shown rather than explained. The middle row keeps the product name, shortened or not, because "workspace" on its own already names the set of folders your window has open. The Aggrega workspace row names the folder the language server anchored to, which is what the Release list is computed against; hovering it gives the full path and, when it differs from the folder you opened, names that one too — so you can find out why the offered Releases are the ones they are. Where your window has exactly one folder open, the Project folder row's hover says it is the only one, rather than leaving you to open a list of one, and closes on what clicking the row offers there — opening a folder, or adding one to the window — and where no Release is selected and nothing has yet read what this Aggrega workspace offers, the hover says that instead of guessing at it. Where a level holds none, the hover names the way out of that state rather than telling you to choose: nothing selected and nothing to select read differently, because only the first is a decision waiting on you. A project holding no Aggrega workspace is answered by opening a folder that holds one or by creating one; an Aggrega workspace holding no Release, by working in a different one or by drafting a Release. The Aggrega workspace and Release rows each carry a **+** at the right, beside the row rather than on it: pressing the row chooses among the ones that exist, and pressing the **+** opens the way to make a new one. The Release **+** opens the same drafting flow as **Draft entity** at the head of the Catalog panel, with the kind already settled: it asks for the name and nothing else, and the prompt says it is naming a Release. The Project folder row carries none — bringing a project folder into being is your editor's business rather than Aggrega's. Where your Aggrega workspace is not the folder you opened — it sits above that folder, or inside it — the Aggrega workspace row carries one further control, which opens that workspace as your project folder. It is offered rather than done for you, and its name says what it costs as well as where it goes: opening a folder reloads the window, so the language server and this extension both restart and anything unsaved in the window goes with them. Where the folder you opened is itself the Aggrega workspace there is nothing to open, and the control is not drawn. When a window opens on a folder whose Aggrega workspace sits outside it — neither that folder nor inside it — the editor also says so in a dialog you dismiss before going on: it opens with **Aggrega is using a workspace from outside the folder you opened.** and, beneath that, an `Aggrega workspace:` line and a `Project folder:` line giving the full path of each. Its buttons are **Open workspace (reloads the window)**, which opens the Aggrega workspace as your project folder just as the row's own control does; **Continue here**, which closes the dialog and changes nothing; and **Don't show again for this folder**. Closing the dialog any other way — with Escape, or with its own close control — is the same as **Continue here**. The dialog appears once for a folder in each window, and again if the Aggrega workspace that folder belongs to changes; after **Continue here** it stays away until the window is reloaded or opened again, and then it returns. **Don't show again for this folder** is remembered for that window and restored when you reopen it, so the dialog does not come back for that folder. None of the three dismisses the fact itself: for as long as the workspace sits outside your folder, the Aggrega workspace row carries a warning mark to the right of its value, and hovering the row gives the same headline and the same two paths the dialog shows. An Aggrega workspace inside the folder you opened is not outside it, so it raises no dialog and its row carries no mark and no such headline; hovering the row still names the folder you opened, and the control opening the workspace as your project folder is still drawn. The dialog is drawn by your operating system unless the editor's `window.dialogStyle` setting is `custom`, so by default it follows your desktop's theme rather than the editor's, and no extension can change how it looks; with `window.dialogStyle` set to `custom` the editor draws it in its own theme. Clicking the Aggrega workspace row opens the choice whatever you have attached, including when that is one workspace or none: the picker lists the Aggrega workspaces your Project folder reaches — walking up from it, and looking through everything inside it — each named by its own root, and, last, a way to reach a folder your window does not have open at all: **Choose another folder Aggrega recognises…**, or **Choose a folder Aggrega recognises…** where the picker has no workspace to list. That last entry is there because reaching is bounded by what your window holds: your editor only ever searches the folders you have open, so a workspace sitting somewhere else is reachable by adding its folder and by nothing shorter. The language server starts as soon as walking up has found somewhere to start, without waiting for that search to finish, so a window can attach and only a moment later report that a second workspace is reachable — the list in the picker catches up when the search returns. The Aggrega workspace this window last worked in is taken again straight away too, one you chose inside your Project folder included, because the editor asks that workspace's own marker rather than waiting on the search; only once its marker has gone, or no longer marks a workspace your Project folder reaches, is the choice dropped, and you are told so. Choosing another entry moves the language server there and says so whether it is reached from the same folder as the one in use or from another, and choosing the entry already in use restarts nothing. One Aggrega workspace reached from two open folders at once is one entry and counts as one: discovery climbs, so a root one level up answers for every folder beneath it, and asking which of those folders holds the workspace would be a question with two true answers. Clicking the Project folder row opens the same kind of choice: the folders your window has open, each named by its own path, and, last, two ways to reach one it does not have. **Open folder…** asks for a folder with your editor's folder dialog, whose button reads **Open**, and opens the folder you pick in this window in place of whatever it has open, as your editor's own Open Folder does. That reloads the window, which the entry's description says beforehand, and if the editor cannot open the folder you are told so. **Add folder to this window…** asks the same way, with a button reading **Add**, and adds the folder you pick to the window, after the ones already open, as the folder the editor works from: you picked it on this row, so the row names it rather than asking you again, and the Aggrega workspaces on offer are the ones it reaches. In a window already open on a workspace file the folder joins it in place, and you are told the editor now works from it. A folder the window already has open is not added again, and you are told so; if the editor refuses the folder, you are told that too, and the editor goes on working from the folder it was. Closing either dialog without picking changes nothing. Adding a folder to a window holding a single folder, or none, makes the window a multi-root workspace, which your editor does by restarting its extensions — this one included — or, in a remote window such as a dev container, by reloading the window. Where the welcome page was open as the extensions restart, it is drawn again in its place, so the window still holds one page and it reads the window as it now is. Both **Add folder to this window…** and the Aggrega workspace picker's last entry end in such an add, so where taking either would do that, its description says so beforehand. That workspace is new to your editor and starts without what the window you left remembered, except for the one answer the add itself gave: a folder added through **Add folder to this window…** is the Project folder there, and an Aggrega workspace chosen through the Aggrega workspace picker's last entry, or through the welcome page's **Use a folder that already has one**, is the Aggrega workspace there. The Release you had chosen, and the folders you had asked the dialog not to show again for, stay with the window you left. Which one you choose is remembered for that window and restored when you reopen it, and it decides what the row beneath offers — the Aggrega workspaces on offer are the ones that folder reaches. Reaching is not the same as containing: because discovery climbs, the workspace a folder reaches is often the folder above it, so choosing a subdirectory of your repository still offers the repository's own workspace. With one folder open there is nothing to choose and the row simply names it. With several and none chosen the row reads **none selected**, and the Aggrega workspaces on offer are the ones the whole window reaches. Where that is one, or where one of them is the one this window last worked in, the language server starts there; where there are several and none of them is remembered, it does not start until you choose one, and the status bar's **Choose Aggrega workspace…** and a notification ask you to. A language server that stops or fails to start on its own leaves the Project folder row naming your folder — your workspace is still chosen, and it is the language-server indicator that reports the server. Below those rows the operations are grouped by what you came to do: **Build** (validate, lint, build, preview, graph), **Dependencies** (pull), **Author** (import, inspect), **Publish** (push, sign, deprecate) and **Configuration** (show config, cache). Alongside Commands sit a **Registries** panel, headed by **Add registry** and **Update index** and listing every registry the effective configuration declares; a **Catalog** panel, headed by **Search catalog** and **Draft entity** and listing the entities the workspace can see; and a **Plugins** panel, headed by **Add plugin** and **Generate entities** and listing the embedded and configured Wasm plugins. Those first rows are part of the panel's own list: each is labelled and carries its icon, so it is visible without pointing at anything, pressing it runs the operation, and collapsing the panel folds it away with the rest. They are there whatever the list below them reads — including when it says nothing is configured, which is exactly when adding the first one is what you came for, and when it says no Aggrega workspace is available. Where one cannot run yet, it stays where it is and says why beside its name, in the words the Commands panel uses for the same state, and pressing it runs nothing. Each of those three panels also carries a refresh in its title bar, which re-reads that one list, and nothing else — an operation there would be an unlabelled icon you had to hover to find. Validate, build, preview build and lint report into the Problems panel; the command-line-backed operations stream their output to the Aggrega output channel.

3efeea12657d5c7a: **It is not in the consuming Recipe's `.features`.** That pillar carries only the attachments written on the component's own block, so a Recipe looking through `.features` for its own attachments by type is never handed a connection's credential. A Recipe reads a connection's attachment from the connection itself, at `.context.uses.<alias>.features.<slot>`, in the shape `.features` carries — its resolved `provides` included (see [A connection's attachments](../templates/template-context-contract.md#a-connections-attachments--contextusesaliasfeatures)).
3f06547fb9e76d03: A FeatureRecipe with `executionScope: boundary` references a per-component-only field such as `.context.instance_id`, `.context.inject`, or `.context.uses` — fields that have no meaningful value at boundary scope — in a template that runs once for the boundary: its `locals:`, `provides:`, `valuesMapping:`, `artifacts:` or a pipeline step's `with:` or `when:`. The mirror condition holds: a component-scope FeatureRecipe (the default) referencing `.boundary.*` fields fails the same validator. Validation runs at parse time against the relevant scope's field allowlist before any rendering work begins. A boundary-scope FeatureRecipe's `injectMapping` is not checked here: it runs once for each component the attachment reaches, in that component's context, so it reads `.context.*`, and a reference to `.boundary` in it is reported by "Template references a root the render context does not define" above.

409a81bcb20904dd: **What an import of a directory reads.** A source may be a directory, and the importer's declared file patterns decide what it reads: the host reads exactly the files of the directory, at any depth, that one of the `files` patterns of the importer's signatures selects — each matched against the end of the file's slash-separated path inside the directory — and hands them over as `sources` in name order, with `bytes` empty and the directory's own name as `name`. A signature declaring no `files` patterns selects no file of a directory, so an importer that declares none reads one file and refuses a directory, and a directory holding no file its patterns select is refused too. The directory is held to itself: a link among the files it would read, or to a directory, that leads out of the directory is refused before anything is read, a link to a directory is never entered, and a link to a file no pattern selects is passed over unread. Recognising a directory's format follows the same rule — each signature is tried against the files its patterns select, in name order, each file read and parsed at most once per syntax, and a signature declaring no pattern applies to none of them. The host caps nothing: a directory too large for the importer is refused by the importer's own runtime limits. None of the compiler's Langflow, Flowise, n8n, Dify and Agent Framework importers declares `files` patterns, so each reads one file; its MCP importer declares the four client configurations' names, so it reads every one of them a directory holds, its Compose importer declares the eight Compose file names, so it is handed every Compose file a directory holds and merges those Compose would read; and its CrewAI importer declares the six names a CrewAI project's declarations are written under, so it is handed a project's declarations and none of its program; and its LangGraph importer declares `langgraph.json`, so it is handed an application's configuration and none of its code or its environment files, an environment file reaching it only under its attachment's `with.sources`; and its Google ADK importer declares `root_agent.yaml`, so it is handed an application's root agent configuration and none of its code or its environment file, the configurations its sub-agents name reaching it only under its attachment's `with.sources`.

42e278ba2c9d6c49: **The Flavored Interfaces (Schema Inheritance):** A Component may declare `extends`, naming another Component as its base, and what that composes is **structure**: labels, annotations, attachment slots, the self-inject allowlist, topology sockets and named `assertions`. The three data pillars do not compose — an extending Component writes the literal marker `schema: inherited` and authors no `values`, `infra` or `provides` content of its own, so its contract is its base's identically. That is why the mechanism **narrows rather than varies**: because the contract is unchanged, every Recipe written for the base already serves the specialization, and the specialization costs one catalog entity and one Manifest mapping line. What a specialization adds is therefore identity a selector or a policy reads — an audit tier, a data zone, a governance contact, or a socket whose selector admits less than the base's. It cannot add a different contract, because it has no surface on which to author one. 455c62d7e22151fc: Map of entry name to artifact-content authoring. Each entry's value carries one of three modes via content-shape dispatch. Mode 1 (inline): a Go template string scalar whose output is the artifact body. Mode 2 (file import): a YAML map of exactly one key, `$import: ./relative/path.yaml`, pointing at a local Go-template file. Mode 3 (library import): a YAML map of exactly one key, `$import: <Library>#/artifacts/<entry>`, referencing an ArtifactLibrary bundle by bare-name identity (the version is supplied by the per-Release lockfile; no registry host appears in the reference). A bundle expands into one output per file, each nested under the entry's key as `<key>/<filename>`. The key names the entry's output: a mode-1 or mode-2 entry's key is its output filename, used as written, and a mode-2 entry's imported file supplies the content without naming the output, so two entries importing different files that share a name are two distinct outputs. Collisions across artifact entries, bundle files, source output, and workload synthesis halt the build when the node renders. The `artifacts` block is authored identically on a Recipe and on a FeatureRecipe — the same three modes, the same key-to-output rule and the same collision behaviour — which is why that part of this description reads the same on both kinds; an example written for one transfers to the other unchanged. In the object form, `$import` must not match `^oci://`; a value that does is rejected. Keys: The key names the entry's output, so it is bounded to a single filename: it begins with a letter or digit and continues with letters, digits, dots, hyphens or underscores. Dots after the first character keep the extensions artifact keys carry (`main.tf`, `template.yaml`, `serviceaccount.yaml`). A `/` would make one key name a path rather than a file, and a leading `.` would admit `..`, which names a location outside the output directory — the first character class refuses both. For a library import the key names the directory the bundle's files are nested under, so the same bound applies. Pattern: `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*$`.

48c27b9b6d9d8be1: Within the workspace and cache tier, `catalog_dirs` is an ordered **first-win precedence stack**. When the same entity identity appears in more than one listed catalog directory, the earlier-listed directory wins and the later occurrence is shadowed — overridden, not loaded, and not an error. This lets a project layer its own catalog directory ahead of a shared or vendored one and override selected entities by identity, while the rest fall through to the shared directory. The override is observable: the resolution detail reports which directory won and which was shadowed, so a layering is never silent. Shadowing applies only *across* directories; two files in a *single* directory that claim the same identity are an authoring mistake and halt the load. A directory named more than once — by a `--catalog` flag and in `catalog_dirs`, or twice in the list — is one entry of the stack, searched once at the place it was first named, so a shadow is always two different files and never a directory read against itself. Because precedence follows the author-controlled directory order, the resolved set is deterministic.

4d0505b0beef2682: **Upstream certificate pinning is the worked case.** A pin is a control over which key an upstream may present: accept only a certificate whose public key matches one the Release supplies. That is a different assertion from requiring an upstream's certificate to chain to a trust anchor the Release supplies, and different again from asserting what a certificate's subject says — both of those state what a certificate must *say*, while a pin states which key it must *be*. **The Deterministic Output Rule (GitOps Safety):**
Because GitOps controllers (ArgoCD, Flux) perform byte-level diff detection on rendered artifacts, the compiler guarantees that identical inputs produce byte-identical outputs. Maps that flow through the template context (`.context.inject.env`, `.values`, `.infra`, and the rest of the runtime view) are backed by ordered-map structures that preserve author insertion order across the data layer; `{{ range }}` over those maps iterates in author order, not in alphabetical order. Ops engineers can rely on iteration order being deterministic across runs of the same input. The Sprig `keys` function, however, returns Go-map iteration order (which is non-deterministic by language design); templates that compose a deterministic key sequence from `keys` output must pipe through `sortAlpha` (e.g., `{{ keys .values | sortAlpha }}`) to recover determinism.

A finding positioned in a module's own document — a refusal of what one of the module's components declares, of a socket its attachments wire, of its values or of the values on its own connections — is published when that module's document is validated, on the key there that wrote it, and on the Aggregate not at all. A finding about the Manifest's mapping table — an entry mapping a type to a Recipe or FeatureRecipe that does not implement it, an entry whose version pin does not parse, or a mapped type whose `extends` chain cannot be followed — is published when that Manifest is validated, on the key of the mapping entry it is about, and on the Aggregate not at all; where the Manifest's open text does not write that entry — an entry it inherits through its own `extends`, or one an unsaved edit removed — the finding is published at the first line of the Manifest. Every other finding the validation of that Release raises is published on the Aggregate: the dependency-level findings that name no document of your workspace — a withdrawn reference or plugin, a catalog Component or Feature whose `extends` chain does not resolve or whose schema is invalid, a gate plugin the trust record does not match, a component instance no mapping resolves, a Recipe or FeatureRecipe whose provider cannot render an input kind it declares, and the schema-pillar-overlap and narrowing-on-extend advisories — among them. So a finding about what the operator wrote appears while the Release is open, one about what a module declares while that module is open, and one about a mapping while the Manifest is open, whichever stage of the build raised it; an editor that validates every open document against the Release shows each there. A Release whose dependencies cannot be resolved at all raises none of those findings, and the failure to resolve them is one entry at the head of the Release's own document and of every other document validated against it that the daemon recognizes, as [Live validation](#live-validation) describes, and does not check as a single entity — its Aggregate, its Manifest, a library, another Release, the workspace configuration — prefixed `Dependencies:` and carrying the resolution's own account of what stopped it. On the Release's own document the entry is that account and nothing more. On every other document it first says that the document is checked against that Release and names the Release as a request names it — `Dependencies: this document is checked against the Release <release>, whose dependencies cannot be resolved:` followed by the account — because nothing in that document says which Release it was checked against: an editor that checks every open document against the one Release selected puts the entry on documents that have nothing to do with that Release, and the name is what tells you the selection is the cause. A file the daemon does not recognize carries no such entry, whatever the Release named with it.

51073acc37ebbac9: **The Solution:** Aggrega replaces hardcoded infrastructure dependencies with **True Control Inversion** via an explicit *Injection Contract*. Developers simply declare a semantic topological edge (e.g., "Agent A uses Database B") and dictate how their code expects to receive the connection data (e.g., as an environment variable or a file mount). The compiler takes the target's Ops-assigned deterministic pointers—whether that is an internal Kubernetes DNS name, a Terraform interpolation string, or a Wasm-formatted DSN—and pipes them directly into the rendering templates without resolving them. This abstracts physical routing and ports away from the developer for modern workloads. The compiler pipes deterministic strings through; stable dependency wiring across environments is a property of Recipe authoring discipline (Ops provides environment-appropriate deterministic pointers), not a guarantee of the core compiler.

52896d83cdaadad0: **Parameter interpolation in an Aggregate** — the `{{ .parameters.<key> }}` references the Aggregate's own text carries — is the earliest of these surfaces: it runs over the raw document before the catalog resolves, so its policy applies to text no other surface has seen yet. 5300f90ac419cbae: Serving a page is then a read of that copy, and it reaches no registry. Before a page is served, the signatures kept beside the copy are verified again under your workspace's check, so a copy another project's looser setting let in is not served to you: where the check pins a key or a trust root that verification runs offline, and where it pins neither — the official hub's built-in check is one such — it obtains the public Sigstore trust root, as a pull does. An offline workspace cannot fetch that trust root, so offline it verifies against the trust root an earlier online fetch on this machine left in the cache the Sigstore client keeps under `.sigstore` in your home directory, however long ago that fetch was, and fetches nothing; on a machine that has never fetched it the check cannot run offline, the copy is not served, and the log stream says so. That verification runs once for each copy and each check while the server runs, and the pages read after it are served on what it admitted: a copy fetched since, a workspace whose check differs — a pinned trust root edited in place included — a read made offline, or an offline read finding a different trust root left on the machine is verified for itself. A copy your check refused is checked again on the next read, so a fetch that has since admitted it is not overruled. If the bundle cannot be acquired, or the only copy is one your check refuses and fetching it again under that check fails, the server still starts and every other surface works; documentation requests answer not-found, and the server's log stream says why.

It renders with every gate on, so a divergence a command-line build would halt on halts here too. A catalog directory the Release reads that cannot be walked — one that is there and cannot be read, say — is refused as [`aggrega build`](aggrega-build.md) refuses it, before anything is written: no artifact, and no lockfile where `autoPull` is set. A directory the workspace configuration lists where nothing exists is read as holding nothing, as `aggrega build` reads it, and the line `aggrega build` prints naming it ([Where local entities are read from](configuration.md#where-local-entities-are-read-from)) travels among the `notices` once: first, under the `catalog` class — or, where the build resolves its dependencies first, among the resolution's own lines under `dependency-resolution`, since that resolution writes the line itself. The refusal is the one `aggrega/irGraph` gives for the same directory, `1004` entity-not-resolvable with the command line's report on one line, and a link leading out of a catalog directory's reads, or out of the documents beside the Release, is refused as `aggrega/irGraph` refuses it, with nothing written. The answer names the `outputDirectory` it wrote to and the `files` it wrote, each relative to that directory and sorted, alongside any `notices` the run raised; findings that carry a document position travel on `aggrega/publishDiagnostics` instead. A Release that refuses while it renders is answered with that refusal in the compiler's words, every cause included, and the refusal is published where it points — see [A refusal raised while rendering](#a-refusal-raised-while-rendering). Where `autoPull` was set, the answer also carries `dependencyResolution`, the same report `aggrega/resolveDependencies` answers with, so a client that filled dependencies as part of the build reads what was pinned without asking again — and where this build's resolution took each reference from, a fact about that run which the lockfile does not record. Each notice carries the `class` of the surface that raised it — `deprecation`, `catalog`, `catalog-lint`, `extends`, `release-composition`, or `dependency-resolution` for a line the dependency resolution below raised — and an empty `class` where the daemon has no name for that surface, which a client renders as the bare `text` rather than guessing at a nearest match. `outputParent` says where inside the workspace the artifacts go, and its name is the whole of what it means: it is the directory the **output directory is created inside**, so sending `docs` writes the artifacts to `docs/dist` rather than into `docs` itself — exactly what a build run in `docs` at a terminal produces. Omit it and the build writes where one run at the workspace root writes. **It reads differently from the `outputDir` the other writing requests here take, and deliberately so:** those name the directory written *into*, this one names that directory's parent, and the two carry different names because they are different things. It is still a destination inside the workspace, so an absolute value, one climbing out of the root, and one leading out of it through a link — a linked directory outside the root, or a directory not made yet beneath one — are refused rather than resolved. 591f720aa43693a6: Build-time cross-field validation. Each entry is a named assertion: the key is a stable rule identifier surfaced in error messages; the value is a Go template string with `{{ fail "message" }}` halt semantics. Multiple named assertions per entity evaluate per-instance in author-declared order; the first failing assertion halts the build. Component assertions evaluate post-resolution, post-analyzer-gate and pre-render, and express architectural invariants of the contract that hold regardless of which Recipe binds. Template context: .values / .infra / .uses / .features / .metadata. The evaluator uses missingkey=error: references to undefined keys halt with a no-such-key diagnostic. Because the bare reference halts before any fallback can run, a plain `default` does not supply an optional-field fallback on this surface — gate the reference with `hasKey`, or use the `optional` helper, which performs the presence check directly. Reading the key through `index` does not supply one either: `index` halts on a map key the map does not hold, naming the key. Inheritance is additive: a Component declaring extends is evaluated against the assertions it inherits as well as its own, with the inherited rules first, and a chain of any depth accumulates from the chain root downward — so when more than one rule would fail, the one declared furthest up the chain is the one reported. Reusing an inherited name to declare a different rule is rejected when the extends chain is resolved against the catalog, naming both Components and the shared name — so it surfaces once the base Component is present, not from the extending document alone; an extending Component adds rules and never replaces one. Restating an inherited rule byte-for-byte under its own name is accepted as the no-op it is. Nothing checks whether two rules can both hold: a mutually unsatisfiable pair is an authoring error that surfaces as an ordinary assertion failure when an instance trips whichever fires first, never as a warning up front.

A port is authored either as the bare port number (`web: 8080`) or as an object carrying the number together with the transport protocol the port carries (`dns: { port: 53, protocol: UDP }`); where no protocol is declared the two forms mean the same thing. The allowed protocol values are `TCP`, `UDP` and `SCTP`, and omitting the key leaves the target's own default in force. Port names are referenced by `services.*.ports` and by an http probe's port resolution, and a service port takes its transport from the container port its name resolves to, so the transport is declared once. K8s: containerPort, carrying protocol only where one is declared. Compose: a container port reaches the output only where a service spec publishes it; the container port itself has no separate compose field, and a published port carries a declared transport as the `/protocol` suffix on the published entry — a transport compose cannot spell halts the build rather than publishing a port that would carry a different one.

The distinction is invitation: an unrequested verdict may not rewrite the build, while an explicitly-attached transform may, because the operator asked for it. Because a transform shapes the rendered output, it is pinned in the lockfile like every output-shaping plugin — the transform that applies is fixed at pull time, so changing it means re-pulling rather than a silent shift between builds; a verdict shapes no output and is not pinned.

The same relation is checked from the Release's side: a boundary entry naming a component the topology does not hold configures nothing, so it halts too and the diagnostic reports the id the entry addressed. `aggrega inspect` and `aggrega pull` share the Release-as-input shape; `aggrega push` takes a catalog entity; `aggrega validate` and `aggrega lint` accept a catalog entity, a Release (via `--release`), or the whole catalog; `aggrega serve` runs as a long-lived process. 5dd8dc4a1b171e49: When two boundaries collapse into one assembly path (shared `directory:`), the merged `docker-compose.yaml` declares one top-level `networks:` entry per contributing boundary. Services from different boundaries within the same compose file can communicate by their service names within compose's default DNS resolution, subject to compose's own cross-network reachability rules. Cross-network L4 routing within a single compose file is what the `compose-bridge` Feature enables: attached at the common-ancestor boundary, it derives a gateway from the boundary's cross-network `uses` edges — generating an `aggrega-gw` service whose nginx `stream` config proxies each bridged edge (one `server` block per edge, on the target's port with a `portBase` collision fallback) and rewriting each consumer's host env var to `aggrega-gw:<port>`. That rewrite replaces the value the consumer's own connection delivered; if another Feature attached to the consumer delivered the same variable, the build halts naming both rather than replace it. The compiler generates that config and delivers it as a **mounted compose config** — a top-level `configs:` entry with inline `content:`, referenced from the gateway and mounted at `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf`; it is not an operator-mounted concern. The `stream` config carries a `resolver` directive and proxies through a per-edge variable (`set $uN <host>; proxy_pass $uN`) so each upstream resolves at connection time rather than once at startup — a bare `proxy_pass` to a not-yet-running target would otherwise fail the gateway at boot. (The `$` in those variables is escaped to `$$` inside `configs.content` so Docker Compose's own `$`-interpolation leaves a literal `$` for nginx.) Inline `configs.content` requires Docker Compose **≥ 2.23.1**. See the [compose-bridge proof case](../entities/featurerecipe.md#compose-bridge-proof-case).

An address is read as the path it names, its percent-escapes decoded, when its authority is empty or `localhost`; one naming another machine is read as that machine's network share on a system that opens a document there that way, and names nothing the daemon can open anywhere else. An address that also carries a query, a fragment, credentials or a port names nothing the daemon can open either. A value that does not open with `file://`, whatever its letter case, is never read as an address, and the file-not-validated refusal names the value you sent, whichever spelling it was. 616c8afedd430f4f: **Selector semantics — the Split Schema mechanism.** `usesSchema[].selector:` is what makes Aggrega's topology more than untyped string-passing. A socket declaring `selector: "datastore.aggrega.ai/engine=vector"` only accepts wiring to Components labeled with the matching key-value pair; an agent attempting to wire its `primary_datastore` socket to a `relational` Component fails the Static Analyzer with a clear selector-violation diagnostic. The selector is a Kubernetes-style label-selector string — comma-AND requirements over `=`, `!=`, `in (...)`, `notin (...)`, bare-key, and `!key` forms — the same grammar Feature `appliesTo` uses; see [vocabulary/modifier-system.md](../vocabulary/modifier-system.md) for the grammar and [architecture/13-catalog-and-registry.md §2 "Kubernetes-Style Selectors"](../../architecture/13-catalog-and-registry.md) for the engine semantics. A requirement outside those forms is refused rather than read as some other selector: an empty requirement (a leading, trailing or doubled comma), a key carrying whitespace or any of `=`, `!`, `(`, `)` and the comma, or a set without its closing parenthesis halts every build that wires an edge through the socket, naming the requirement. So a socket meant to exclude frontends is written `selector: "tier!=frontend"`; `"!tier=frontend"` is refused, because `!` names a label key and nothing else.

A parent Aggregate can declare a child Aggregate exactly like a component, passing `parameters` down into it. To prevent tight coupling, child Aggregates expose an **`exportedComponents:`** contract, establishing a stable public interface name. The parent requests this interface, and the Go compiler dynamically rewires the topological edge to the correct internal node. A module may itself re-export a nested module's exported component under its own interface name — optionally renaming it — and the compiler resolves such a re-export chain transitively to the underlying internal node, so modules compose to any depth without a parent needing to know how deeply the target is nested. 65aefd1281b9c98d: **A required signature the lockfile does not record.** Where the trust configuration requires a signature for a dependency the cache serves and the lockfile row records none — the row was edited, the lockfile was written afresh over a cache an earlier pull filled, or the requirement was added after the pull that wrote the row — the re-pull asks that dependency's registry for its signature, by the digest of the manifest stored beside it in the cache, exactly as it does for a dependency it fetches, and records the verified signature on the row. That row is the one a build refuses ([No verified signature is recorded for an artifact that requires one](../errors/fatal-halts.md#no-verified-signature-is-recorded-for-an-artifact-that-requires-one)), so pulling again is what clears that refusal. A registry that attaches no signature, or a signature the trust configuration does not accept, halts the re-pull as it halts a pull that fetched the dependency. The settings that let a pull admit a dependency with no signature leave such a row as it is and ask nothing about it: `skip_signature_verification` at the top level, the same switch on the registry's own entry except for a kind the workspace-wide signing policy requires, and a registry marked `advisory`.

Every other key configures the listener the HTTP transport starts and is not used while the server speaks over standard input and output — `listen` included, which is read there only so the server can say, in one line on its error stream, that the address is not used. Each key below says which it is. Distinct from `serve`, which configures the editor-backend daemon.
65b35a0560177f19: `aggrega/irGraph` — the compiled IR graph for a Release, for editor introspection. `release` is a path relative to the workspace root, naming a Release inside it — the same value `aggrega build --release` takes when run from the root. Any other form is refused with the standard invalid-params error naming what to send instead: an absolute path, a path that resolves outside the workspace root — whether it climbs out as written or leads out through a link, to the file or to a directory on the way — and an empty value are all rejected rather than resolved, so a request never reports on a file the workspace does not hold. A Release your workspace configuration names, as `build.authoring_release` or as a key of `workspace.releases`, is one the workspace holds wherever its file sits, so a link inside the workspace leading to it is accepted, as `aggrega/releaseCandidates` lists it. A catalog directory the Release reads that cannot be walked — one that is there and cannot be read, say — is refused as [`aggrega inspect`](aggrega-inspect.md) refuses it, before anything else is read: the error is `1004` entity-not-resolvable, its message is the report the command line prints for that directory, on one line (`[CATALOG_ERROR] <directory>: catalog load: …`), and no graph is drawn over the directories that remain. A directory the workspace configuration lists where nothing exists is not refused: it is read as holding nothing, as every command reads it ([Where local entities are read from](configuration.md#where-local-entities-are-read-from)), and the graph is the one drawn without it. A catalog directory holding a link that leads out of the directory its reads must stay inside — a document or a directory linked from elsewhere, beneath a catalog directory inside the workspace or beneath one the configuration names outside it — is refused the same way and at the same moment, with `1004` and the condition's own sentence naming the link and where it leads: nothing is read through such a link, and a graph drawn without it could resolve another entity of the same name in its place. So is a link leading out among the documents beside the Release, where the Release names its Aggregate or its Manifest by identity. A file the Release, its Manifest or a Release it extends names by a path — `aggregate:`, `manifest:`, `extends:` or a parameters `$import:` — that leads out of the workspace, as written or through a link, is refused with the condition's own sentence ([fatal-halts.md](../errors/fatal-halts.md) §"A reference to another file leads out of the directory it must stay inside"), the error's data placing it on the key in the Release that led to the file, and nothing is read from that file; a Release the configuration names outside the workspace is held the same way to the directory holding it, so a path it or a Release its chain leads to writes that leaves that directory is refused too. Note that `aggrega/releaseCandidates` answers with absolute paths, so a client feeding one surface from the other converts between the two. That this parameter refuses a spelling the per-document `file` and `uri` parameters accept is deliberate, and [Which spellings a parameter you send accepts](#which-spellings-a-parameter-you-send-accepts) says what decides it. The graph withholds every value an author declared sensitive, exactly as `--ir-graph` withholds it on the command line: each is replaced by the marker [`aggrega-inspect`](aggrega-inspect.md#machine-readable-output) "Machine-readable output" describes, and everything else is carried as the compiler recorded it. `unredacted: true` asks for those values in the clear — the protocol's spelling of the command line's `--unredacted`, and the one way to ask; absent or `false`, the answer withholds them. Whatever the answer reaches then carries the values in the clear, so a client asks for them only where the person using it has.

65e179c7f9338737: **Mapping is deterministic, confidence-scored, and weighed against your own catalog.** The host hands the importer a view of the Components the workspace's own catalog holds — the catalog the importer was selected from — the workspace's catalog folders, or, where it names none, the catalog snapshot its default registry publishes — an enterprise catalog's Components exactly as the standard library's. The view carries each Component's name, version and labels, the key names its values and provides declare, and the selectors of its sockets, and never a value, a default or a secret; nothing is fetched for it beyond that snapshot, and its order is fixed, so one catalog yields one view. An importer built on the Go PDK's importer package — the compiler's own Langflow, Flowise, n8n and Compose importers among them — weighs each node in the source against those Components and nothing else, with a deterministic, no-model confidence model, and records the decision — the candidates it weighed, the match tier it assigned, and the choice it made — as reviewable hints an author can read and revise. A Component the catalog gains is a candidate on the next import, with no importer rebuilt. The default is hints only: the import proposes, and the author decides. A high-confidence match can be written as a reference to an existing catalog component instead of a freshly drafted body, but only when the operator opts in — always as an explicit, reversible suggestion the author gates, never a silent rewrite. Because the scoring carries no model and no runtime lookup, the same source scored against the same catalog always produces the same hints.

672c67b809dbb1b4: **Schema Agnosticism (open source dictionary):** The core compiler is agnostic to physical execution layers. It does not possess hardcoded schemas for Helm, Terraform, or Docker Compose. Instead, the `source` block of an Ops Recipe is an open dictionary whose keys are provider-defined and surface to the Recipe's templates as `.source.*`. The design direction is that each provider's Wasm socket defines and validates its own source shape — so enterprises can introduce new infrastructure tools without waiting for core schema updates; that per-provider Wasm source validation is not yet implemented. Today the core resolves a *fetched* source by a built-in `{ kind, url, version }` form (kinds: `helm-oci-chart`, `helm-https-chart`, `compose-https-fragment`, `git-repository`), which already decouples the compiler from the cloud languages it manipulates. 6789fc6e78c2da3f: **Envoy Gateway in front of models:** `core/gateway/envoy-gateway`, the open-source Envoy Gateway, serves the models wired to its own `models` socket through Envoy AI Gateway, whose controller, `core/gateway/envoy-ai-gateway-operator`, the gateway calls as its extension server through its `extension` socket. A model wired with nothing on that socket halts the build, and with the controller wired the Release places the gateway in `envoy-gateway-system` or the build halts. Each wired model becomes a rule of one AI route attached to the gateway, chosen by the model name a request carries, with a backend written from the `endpoint` and `model` the model publishes, so every wired model is served under `/v1` at the gateway's own address. The gateway presents each connection's own credential as a bearer token, which Envoy AI Gateway's controller reads from the Secret the credential names, and a connection reaching a model whose `model.aggrega.ai/api` is not `openai` halts the build. While a model is wired, every route on the gateway takes the 50Mi per-connection request buffer Envoy AI Gateway configures. It publishes its address, qualified with `envoy-gateway-system` so it resolves from any namespace, as its `endpoint` and the alias its `values.model` names as its `model`, and carries `model.aggrega.ai/api: openai`, so an agent's `model` socket takes it as it takes the AI gateway; with nothing wired it publishes both keys empty. The controller's webhook serves a certificate cert-manager issues, so cert-manager must already run in the cluster, unless the Release names, in the controller's `infra.webhook_tls_secret`, a Secret holding a certificate the operator supplies, which the webhook then serves. 69d035c9db494557: **Wire encoding.** A step's input (`FRPStepInput`) and its answer (`FRPStepOutput`) travel as **canonical CBOR** ([RFC 8949](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8949) §4.2.1), in both directions. A guest decodes its input and encodes its answer through the entry points the payload types carry — `DecodeCBOR` and `EncodeCBOR` in Go, `decode_cbor` and `encode_cbor` in Rust (on the types the `aggrega-abi` crate publishes), `decodeCBORFRPStepInput` and `encodeCBORFRPStepOutput` in TypeScript — reading and writing bytes (`Vec<u8>` in Rust, `Host.inputBytes()` and `Host.outputBytes(...)` in TypeScript). No CBOR library is needed and nothing hand-parses bytes. The step's `with` input (`step_input`), the `outputs` it returns, and the `own` and `host` document sets are maps the schema marks order-preserving, so they cross as [ordered lists of entries](#maps-that-keep-their-order) in the order the pipeline holds them, and a guest reads and writes them through its kit's order-keeping container — which is what lets a step's outputs reach `.steps.<id>.outputs` in the order the step returned them. Each unit's `tree`, each value of `step_input` and `outputs`, a patch's `value`, a side effect's `crd` and the render `context` cross as the bytes of their JSON documents, which a guest parses as JSON to look inside; a unit's `bytes` cross as a raw byte run the generated decoder fills into the kit's own field type — a byte slice in Go, a base64 string in Rust and TypeScript. Each diagnostic crosses in the shared `Diagnostic` shape. An answer that is not an `FRPStepOutput` in this encoding — one written as JSON, or one carrying a top-level field the shape does not declare — fails the step, naming the function it runs, which halts the build unless the step is `optional`. Called directly with `aggrega plugin run-local --export step`, a step is handed the authored JSON payload converted into this encoding, and its answer is written out as the bytes it returned.

6d39770ec3f2cb1c: **The host runtime: a capability-denying sandbox.** Aggrega embeds the Wasm host as the Extism toolkit running on top of the Wazero engine; the host binary stays pure Go with no native toolchain dependency, so `aggrega` cross-compiles cleanly. Every socket runs behind an **AOT-purity firewall**: the host refuses to grant a plugin any runtime-access capability — no network, no filesystem, no wall-clock, no environment, no standard I/O — and rejects a plugin that asks for one. A plugin that cannot reach the network or read the clock cannot break the compiler's ahead-of-time guarantee that the same input produces the same output. Language runtimes that need a few benign startup imports run against a capability-denied configuration of those imports: the host fixes the observable wall clock, supplies real entropy, discards standard I/O, and grants no filesystem, argument, or environment access — so a plugin can reach no host capability that varies across builds. Entropy is deliberately left real rather than pinned: pinning it would stabilise a guest language runtime's internal hash seed and map-iteration order, and so hide a plugin whose own output is not reproducible instead of letting that surface as differing output. A plugin whose result depends on entropy is an authoring-level determinism problem, and this configuration is built to reveal it rather than mask it.

**Stating a rule once: governance attachments are workspace-scoped.**
The two patterns above are authored per component and per Feature, but the governance attachment that enforces them is not. A governance plugin is attached at the workspace configuration's `plugins.governance` key, and that attachment binds **every build in the workspace**. A corporate rule is therefore stated in exactly one place: the platform team attaches the plugin once, and no component, Aggregate or Release has to opt in, mention it, or be edited for it to apply. This is what makes the validation failsafe in pattern 1 a complete answer rather than a per-project convention — a developer who bypasses the internal catalog and requests a naked `core/postgres` is evaluated by the same attached policy as everyone else, because the policy is a property of the workspace rather than of the component they chose.

7000483027a021f9: **Why every catalog YAML repeats the envelope.** The envelope (`apiVersion`, `kind`, `metadata` block) appears at the top of every catalog file — Component, Feature, Recipe, FeatureRecipe, Aggregate, Manifest, Release, Plugin — regardless of how short the body is. The repetition is deliberate: each file is designed to parse, validate, lint, and inspect as a standalone artefact. A single file pulled from the OCI registry, dropped into a CI sandbox, or opened in a third-party editor must carry enough self-description that downstream tooling can identify what kind of entity it represents and which schema version applies. Catalog-relative-path inference (where the directory location implies the entity kind and the envelope could be omitted) is not implemented today — every parser, validator, and linter consumes the envelope explicitly. The cost is mechanical boilerplate per file; the benefit is that the standalone-tooling guarantee holds across the OCI distribution surface, the local filesystem, and the IDE / CI / inspect surfaces. Authors copy the envelope from existing files when authoring new catalog content; future scaffolders are expected to ship the boilerplate as starter templates.

71035fd162b6c233: **`artifacts:` (artifacts) — available.** The field is a map of named entries; each entry is authored inline or loaded via per-entry `$import:`. 7143da7934d874d6: **Which plugins are pinned, and which your environment chooses.** Aggrega splits plugins by whether they change the output you ship. Gate plugins — policy and lint — judge a build without changing its bytes, so they are cached at pull (so a build can still run them offline; one the compiler binary carries, or one authored in your own catalog directory, is read from there instead) but not pinned: which gate runs is chosen by your environment at build time, so a dev-permissive / CI-strict split is an ordinary configuration choice rather than a re-pull, and switching gates never changes the output a passing build emits. Furthermore, to support OCI registry discoverability and lifecycle governance, the `metadata` block supports an optional **Enterprise Metadata Suite**. One name evaluated to the same bytes — by two components bound to one Recipe, or by two Recipes configuring one provider identically — is one file. One name evaluated to different bytes stops the build, naming the file and every contributor, because no single file is what all of them wrote; so does a name the provider's own assembly writes, such as `aggrega.modules.tf`. Both are the [assembled-output collision](../errors/fatal-halts.md#two-contributors-write-the-same-output-path). Two Recipes configuring one provider under two different file names are not merged — each file is written — and the target is what then reports the duplicate configuration, so Recipes meant to share a provider configuration share its file name, conventionally one named for the provider it configures.

The official hub, `hub.aggrega.ai`, limits how many requests may come from one address in a
short span, so machines sharing an address share that allowance, and any registry may limit
its clients the same way. A registry past its limit answers `429 Too Many Requests`, or
`503 Service Unavailable` with a `Retry-After` header saying how long to wait. Every request
the command line makes to a registry, whatever the command, meets that answer the same way:
it waits as long as the registry asked, or ten seconds where the answer does not say, plus up
to a second more at random, and then asks again, with no fixed number of attempts. Every
request to that registry waits with it, not only the one refused, and fewer are sent to it at
once — half as many each time it asks, down to one — rising again by one after each run of
requests it serves without failing, back to the command's usual number. The wait is shown on the same terms as the rest of the
command's progress, as a line such as `hub.aggrega.ai asked to slow down; waiting 11 s`:
`aggrega build`, `aggrega pull` and `aggrega registry update` show it beside the step in
flight, the other commands that show what they wait on show it as a step of its own — except
`aggrega sign --jobs` signing several references at once, which shows them as one step — and

The Go CLI natively reads it to extract the `selector:` strings for label matching during static analysis and to validate allowed `inject` mechanisms. Each socket entry supports an optional `required: true` field (default `false`) — when set, the compiler emits a validation error if no dependency is declared in that socket. This is the soft equivalent of the `required: true` semantics on `featuresSchema` entries. Declaring a socket here is what the standard-library catalog does and remains the better path — but it is not the only way a developer can draw an edge. An Aggregate author may name a socket on their own component that this `usesSchema` does not declare, including on an entity that declares no `usesSchema` at all; such an ad-hoc socket carries no selector, no `inject` allowlist and no per-edge schema, precisely because there is no entry here to carry them. A Feature attachment's `uses` and a Release's per-edge `uses` are not open that way — both may only name a declared socket. See [dependency-resolution §"Domain 2: The Split Schema"](07-dependency-resolution.md) for the full contract and what an ad-hoc socket gives up.

7c8f2c1cfc1fd399: **Two answers a target can give, and they lead different places.** Where a shorter name would be accepted, the halt states the length that would work, so a new name is chosen once rather than twice. Where no length would help — a character the target's grammar refuses in the position it landed in — no length is stated, because shortening cannot reach it. The most common case of the second kind: a target whose names are lowercase-only escapes each character it does not admit, and every escape begins with a hyphen, so a name whose *first* character is escaped produces a name beginning with a hyphen. A target requiring a lowercase letter or a digit there refuses it however short the rest is. A target may also hold the start of a name to the stricter rule of the resources named after it: the helm target refuses a name beginning with a digit, reported as a `Service name`, because Helm accepts such a release name while the cluster refuses a Kubernetes Service named after it.
7c905f7694d06c5f: **Topological Dependency Mapping (`uses`):** Where an AI framework wires an agent to its tools or to a vector datastore, that wiring dictates *who talks to whom*, so it is declared in the `uses` pillar; a list of names kept in `values`, such as the standard library's `tools_allowed`, is a convention that draws no edge. The compiler draws these explicit edges in the IR Graph verbatim. This allows downstream Wasm rendering plugins to programmatically generate the network policies and physical boundaries required to secure the connections, without the compiler understanding the underlying AI framework.

It is the **Import** button in the Commands panel's Author group too, and **Import into Aggrega** on a file or a folder's right-click menu in the Explorer, which imports the file or folder you clicked: the three are one command, so they ask the same questions, in this order, each in the editor's own input, except that the Explorer entry does not ask for the source. First the source: **File…** or **Folder…**, then your editor's open dialog for one of that kind — the choice comes first because on Windows and Linux one dialog cannot offer both. Then the folder inside the workspace to draft into, relative to its root, where leaving it empty drafts beneath the workspace root, as `aggrega import` does without `--output-dir`. Then the options, a list in which you may tick **Preview**, **Sync**, both or neither: **Preview** is `--dry-run` — nothing is written, and each file the import would write is shown on the output channel followed by its content — and **Sync** is `--sync`, bringing what an earlier import drafted up to date with the source, changing only what the import wrote, with each part it brings up to date listed on the channel in the words `aggrega import --sync` prints for it; ticking neither writes the drafts whole. Last, the provider capability to draft a Manifest for, such as `compose` or `helm`, where leaving it empty drafts none, as without `--target`. An answer you leave empty, and an option you leave unticked, is not sent at all, so the compiler applies its own default, and dismissing any question or dialog ends the import with nothing sent. A folder that leads out of the workspace, and a capability no Recipe in the workspace's catalog binds to, are refused by the compiler in its own words before anything is written. The format is recognised from the source's own shape, as at a terminal; where the compiler refuses because no format, or more than one, recognises the source, the editor shows that refusal — which names the formats — and asks for the format to read the source as, then sends the same import again carrying it, and leaving that question empty ends the import with the refusal. It reads the file you name, or the files of the directory you name that its importer reads, and no others. It reaches no network, except the first time a format needs one of the compiler's core importers this machine does not hold yet: that import fetches it from the workspace's default registry, verifies it and keeps it in the content cache, as `aggrega import` does. The source may sit anywhere on this machine, because it is a file you pointed at rather than one the workspace holds; the drafts always land in the workspace. It shows progress with a Cancel button, and pressing Cancel stops the conversion rather than only stopping the editor waiting, because the importer runs as a plugin the compiler can unwind mid-run. The ending says what the source was recognised as, how many files were drafted and where they went, counting the drafts and not `.aggrega-import.json`, the record of what the import wrote that every import writes beside its drafts; the importer's own findings and every file that reached disk, the record included, go to the Aggrega output channel, because they name a place in the source file rather than in a document you authored.

7d29cbbb10ba0b7e: **How to fix:** run the pull the message names. For an entry the content cache serves that records no signature where one is required, the pull asks the artifact's registry for its signature, by the manifest digest the entry records, exactly as it does for an artifact it fetches, and records the verified signature on the entry — so the next build reads it. A plugin attached at a verdict role is asked about on every pull in any case, and the pull records what it verified on the plugin's entry in `plugins-trust.yaml`, creating the entry where there is none. A registry that attaches no signature, or a signature the trust configuration does not accept, halts that pull instead, naming the artifact, and that is a question for whoever publishes it. Under the offline posture the pull cannot ask: over a lockfile entry it refuses naming how to allow the network for one run, and over a plugin attached at a verdict role it stops before asking, naming the plugin's `.wasm` as one it could not resolve, because a pull resolves that `.wasm` from the plugin's registry. Restoring the entry's recorded signature from version control clears it without the network, where the cache still holds the signature material that record names. Where the artifact is not meant to be signed, the requirement is the thing to change, and the message names which setting it is — but relaxing it means that registry's artifacts are no longer checked at a pull either, so prefer narrowing the workspace-wide policy's kinds over switching a requirement off.

7d33a7f08d62f9e6: **Connection credential matches target key** (`connection-credential-matches-target-key`) — a server that checks a key holds the key it verifies in a slot of its own Component, and a caller presents a key on the connection it reaches the server through. Neither end sees the other's attachments, so the two hold one key only because their authors write it at both ends — usually by having both attachments read one parameter — and a build never compares them. This rule does, and it is the one rule that reads a whole Release, so it runs under `--release` and at no other scope. It finds both ends by the names the standard catalog gives them: the target's key is the slot `api_key` its Component declares in `spec.featuresSchema`, and the caller's is the slot `credential` on the connection, written at `uses.<socket>.<alias>.features.credential` in the Aggregate or on a connection the Release wires. For each connection whose target declares `api_key` and is not labelled managed, it reports a connection carrying a credential to a target whose key slot is unfilled, a filled key slot with no credential on the connection, and two ends naming their secret differently. What it compares is each end's locator — the `origin` an attachment writes, in `values` in the Aggregate or `infra` in the Release — as the author wrote it, so two ends reading one parameter compare equal and two literals compare by their text; nothing is resolved, and a finding names the component, the connection, the target and the two slots but **never quotes either locator**, since the text written there can be the secret itself. A target declaring no `api_key` slot draws nothing, and a slot that is not the caller key, such as a model server's registry pull token, is never read. Nor is a target whose Component is labelled `component.aggrega.ai/hosting: managed` judged, whatever its `api_key` slot holds: such a Component stands for a service its vendor runs, so nothing the Release runs checks a key on it, and where it declares `api_key` — the key to a hosted model API, say, under the name the vendor's product gives it — the slot holds the key the Release presents to that vendor, never one its callers present. A target labelled `self-hosted`, `external` or `mixed`, or carrying no hosting label, is judged. A connection on the socket `scrape_target` — the name the standard catalog gives the socket a metrics scraper reaches its targets through — is a scrape, and whether a scrape's credential should be the target's caller key depends on the target's product: some serve their metrics with no credential, some put them behind the key every caller presents, and some take a token of their own. So for a scrape the rule reads what the target's Component states in its annotation `observability.aggrega.ai/metrics-credential`: under `none` the scrape is not judged at all; under `separate-token` its credential is never compared with the target's `api_key`, so none of the three findings is reported on it; under `target-key` it is judged like any other connection. The rule reads only those three values, so a scrape to a target without the annotation, or with any other value, is judged like any other connection — and every connection on another socket, a model, tool or datastore connection included, is judged the same whatever the target's annotation says. It reads the attachments written on the target and on the connection: an `api_key` attachment reaching the target from a subsystem or a boundary instead leaves that connection unjudged, one an annotation adds is not among them, so a key slot filled only that way reads as unfilled, an end whose attachment writes no locator is compared only for whether it is filled, and a component an imported module contributes is not read. Because the slot names, the hosting label, the scrape socket's name and the metrics annotation are catalog conventions no schema keyword marks, a catalog naming the slots differently draws nothing, a scraping socket named differently is judged like any other socket, and a Component that holds a vendor's key in a slot named `api_key` without the managed label is read as a target checking that key, since the slot's name, the label and the annotation are all the rule reads of a target's Component. Default on; opt out with `allow_connection_credential_mismatches`.

The bundle read is the one published for the version of `aggrega` you are running; where none is published for that version, it is the newest one published for an earlier release — the same choice [`aggrega scaffold --example`](aggrega-scaffold.md#starting-from-a-runnable-example) makes, so the two never read different documentation. That check also runs offline. Where it pins a key or a trust root it reads only those; where it pins neither, as the official hub's built-in check does, it verifies against the public Sigstore trust root, which an offline workspace cannot fetch — so offline it verifies against the trust root an earlier online fetch on this machine left under `.sigstore` in your home directory, and fetches nothing. When the machine has no copy, or none your check admits, the command acquires one under that check, once, and reads from the cache afterwards. The same copy serves the documentation an assistant reads through [`aggrega mcp`](aggrega-mcp.md) and the explanations an editor shows through [`aggrega serve`](aggrega-serve.md).

Object and array slots recurse: each entry under `properties` and each element against `items` is checked the same way, a `valuesType` contract governs the keys `properties` does not name, and a nested key no declaration names is rejected. Platform Ops engineers must **never** hardcode physical cloud resource names. It has no default: when unset, no timestamp authority is contacted, and a keyless signature's trusted time comes from its transparency-log entry. It is written as an absolute `https` URL: `https://`, a host, and optionally a port and a path, with no whitespace — for example `https://tsa.example.com/api/v1/timestamp`. A value in any other shape, such as one with no scheme (`tsa.example.com`) or one beginning `http://`, is refused when the configuration file loads, naming the file and the key. 8a2e41ff7e0b2b15: Cap on the bytes the compiled-module cache holds on disk. Default 53687091200 (50 GiB), a ceiling that stops unbounded growth rather than a budget meant to be felt — a single compiled plugin reaches hundreds of megabytes, so a machine that builds many plugin versions accumulates gigabytes. Set it above what one build compiles: the cap is applied before a build compiles anything, so a cap below a single build's own working set makes every build discard and recompile the same modules, and the store stops saving anything. Because the cap is applied first and the build then writes what it compiles, the store can sit above the cap between builds; it is trimmed again at the start of the next one. `0` disables the cap (the store grows without bound and nothing is ever removed automatically). Because the store is one directory every workspace shares, this cap is not per-project even when a project's own file carries it: the value resolves the same way every other key does, with the nearer file winning, but the store still has only one size. The cap in force is the one from the most recent build, so two projects capping it differently both take effect in turn, and a low cap in one discards machine code the other compiled. Setting it once in the global config file is what gives the whole machine one answer. `aggrega config show --origin` names the file each setting's effective value came from. Default: `53687091200`

**`ir-verdict`** — the guest reasons over the intermediate-representation
  graph, before rendering. The payload carries the full capability-agnostic IR graph (every
  node, edge, and attachment the compiler holds) plus the routing paths the
  analyzer enumerates, so a policy can reason about topology and reachability
  without re-walking the graph. That path list is **bounded per starting node** —
  a densely connected or cyclic topology can hold more distinct routes than the
  enumeration emits, and once the bound is reached the remaining routes from that
  starting node are not listed. A path that is present is therefore real, while
  the absence of a path is not proof that none exists: a policy whose verdict
  turns on something being *unreachable* should establish that from the nodes and
  edges, which the payload carries in full, rather than from the path list alone.
  One thing in the graph is not as written: every value an author declared
  sensitive — in an attachment's `values` or `infra`, in a boundary
  attachment's `infra`, in a node's own `values` or `infra`, or in a
  connection's own `values` or `infra` — arrives as the
  withheld marker `{"aggrega_withheld": "declared"}`, while its key, its
  sensitivity marking and every undeclared value beside it arrive as written. A
  policy judges where declared-sensitive material travels and never receives the
  material; see
  [the attachment facts a governance policy reads](governance-attachment-facts.md#declared-sensitive-values-arrive-withheld).
  An `ir-verdict` policy runs at the static-analysis
  gate, before any artifacts are produced. Use it for policies about
  architecture and wiring — topology invariants, cross-boundary auth,
  credential-flow shape — that should halt a build before it renders anything.
8a40c14c4d250804: **An identity that opens as a composed one does.** Resources a Feature emits cannot be stamped with a component name you wrote, so Aggrega composes an identity for them out of the parts you did write, behind a fixed opening that says where the Feature was attached. Where the Feature is attached to a **single component**, the identity is composed from that component and the key the Feature is attached under, and it opens with `cfr--`. Where it is attached to a whole **boundary**, no one component's name applies at all, so the identity is composed from the path of the boundary and the name the Feature is attached under, and it opens with `bfr--`. The opening is what tells a reader which of the two a resource came from, rather than from a component. **So `bfr--` and `cfr--` are both reserved at the start of a component identity.** A component named `bfr--api` or `cfr--api` would be stamped identically to a composed one, and nothing in the emitted output could tell the two apart. Only the full opening is reserved: a component named `bfr`, `cfr`, `bfr-api` or `bfrontend` is an ordinary name and builds.

8c37868db2139034: The selector is held to its grammar at the moment it is evaluated, which is once for every edge wired through the socket. A selector the engine cannot read as one of its six requirement forms — an empty requirement left by a stray comma, a key carrying whitespace or one of the characters the grammar uses to tell its forms apart (`=`, `!`, `(`, `)` and the comma), or a set without its closing parenthesis — halts the build on that edge, naming the requirement, instead of being read as some other selector. The strictness is what keeps the check honest: read leniently, `!tier=frontend`, written to keep frontends out, would ask only that no label be *named* `tier=frontend`, and every target — frontends included — would pass. The same grammar governs attachment-slot selectors and a Feature's `appliesTo`; [the selector grammar](../language-reference/vocabulary/modifier-system.md) lists every form and every refusal. A build never evaluates a socket no edge is wired through, so `aggrega validate` — over the whole catalog, or over the Component or Feature declaring the socket — reads every declared socket's selector and refuses a malformed one there, under the code and in the words a build that wires the socket uses.

8c5c3c597de60b4a: Header the proxy in front puts the caller's identity in — for example `X-Forwarded-User`. It is written as an HTTP header name: letters, digits and hyphens, and the other characters a header name may carry (`!#$%&'*+.^_\|~` and the backtick), with no space, colon or other separator. A name in any other shape is refused when the configuration file loads, naming the file and the key, because no request can carry such a header. An empty one is refused too: it would leave this server checking tokens itself while the block says a proxy in front does. To leave this mode off, leave `trusted_proxy` out. The header's value is taken exactly as written and compared to nothing, in the same way the subject of a token this server validates itself is recorded and compared to nothing. It is the whole credential in this mode, so it is required whenever `trusted_proxy` is set, and a request arriving without it is answered `401`. Pattern: ``^[!#$%&'*+.^_`\|~0-9A-Za-z-]+$``.
