8d1bac746ba2d88a: Optional per-boundary deployment wave (signed integer, default 0). Every component in this boundary inherits the boundary's wave into its node. Negative values are permitted (run before everything else); larger values run after lower ones. On K8s and Helm the wave is what orders the deployment: it becomes an `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave` annotation, and on a resource the chart already marks as a Helm hook it also becomes that hook's `helm.sh/hook-weight`. On compose the wave both is recorded as a service label and orders the services of the file it renders into, through `depends_on` between them — so it reaches every service in that one file and nothing outside it. On cloudformation the wave orders provisioning of the stack the boundary assembles into: every resource in a wave is declared to depend on the resources of the wave before it, which fixes the order they are created in and, in reverse, the order they are deleted in. That is creation and deletion order only — a stack template expresses no notion of a resource being ready, so nothing waits for one to become serviceable. On terraform the wave orders the module blocks of the root configuration the boundary assembles into: every module in a wave is declared to depend on the modules of the wave before it, which fixes the order the engine performs its actions in. That is action order only — a configuration expresses no notion of a resource being ready, so nothing waits for one to become serviceable — and the value is also recorded with the node's build provenance. On arm the wave orders deployment of the template the boundary assembles into, declaring every resource and nested deployment in a wave to depend on those of the wave before it through `dependsOn`. The compiler carries the same value onto every node in the boundary as that node's `sync_wave`, where the per-target behaviour is described again from the node's side. Nested boundaries do not implicitly inherit — each declares its own wave.

8d21332250ee1308: **Which plugins are pinned, and which your environment chooses.** Aggrega splits plugins by whether they change the output you ship. Output-shaping plugins — the render providers, the mutator, and the FeatureRecipe and Recipe pipeline steps — are pinned in the release lockfile when you `aggrega pull`, and reproduced byte-identically at `aggrega build` and `aggrega serve` from that lockfile alone. Two kinds are not pinned, because a build reads each from the same place every time: a render provider served from inside the compiler binary, and a provider or pipeline step whose `Plugin` entity is authored in one of your own catalog directories. To change which output-shaping plugin applies, you re-pull; a change to your workspace configuration after a pull does not move a build's output until the next pull. Gate plugins — policy and lint — judge a build without changing its bytes, so they are cached at pull (so a build can still run them offline; one the compiler binary carries, or one authored in your own catalog directory, is read from there instead) but not pinned: which gate runs is chosen by your environment at build time, so a dev-permissive / CI-strict split is an ordinary configuration choice rather than a re-pull, and switching gates never changes the output a passing build emits. Plugins that act only on authoring input, such as importers and CLI extensions, shape no build output and are neither pinned nor part of the build's cached set.

Resolving a plugin only reads what is already on the machine and fetches nothing, so this condition reports that none of the four holds the bytes — not that a download failed. **One plugin is the exception: a [core importer](../plugins/core-importers.md) an import needs.** Its module is read from the binary or the content cache alone, never from beside a catalog entity, and where neither holds it the import fetches it once from the workspace's default registry; the condition then reports that the fetch was not possible as well — the workspace is offline, its registry could not be reached or does not hold the module, or the workspace names no default registry. A module that was fetched and does not verify is refused under its own condition instead, a digest mismatch or a signature refusal, and nothing is kept.

8d28727014d2b7d9: **Wire encoding.** The input and the output both travel as **canonical CBOR** ([RFC 8949](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8949) §4.2.1), the encoding the same `ParseInput` travels in when a guest hands it to `aggrega_parse_source`. A guest decodes its input and encodes its output through the entry points its kit's `ParseInput` and `ParseOutput` already carry — `DecodeCBOR` and `EncodeCBOR` in Go, `decode_cbor` and `encode_cbor` in Rust, `decodeCBORParseInput` and `encodeCBORParseOutput` in TypeScript — reading and writing bytes (`Vec<u8>` in Rust, `Host.inputBytes()` and `Host.outputBytes(...)` in TypeScript). No CBOR library is needed and nothing hand-parses bytes. The source bytes cross as a raw byte run, and the generated decoder fills them into the kit's own field type: a byte slice in Go, a base64 string in Rust and TypeScript. `options` and `tree` cross as the bytes of their JSON documents, so the tree a parser writes reaches its consumer verbatim. A parser that cannot complete says why in the output's `error`, and the parse fails naming the parser and that message; an answer that is not a `ParseOutput` in this encoding — one written as JSON, or one carrying a top-level field the shape does not declare — fails the parse too, naming the parser and its `parse` export. A failed parse halts a build at the render-verdict role, and reaches an importer as the failure `aggrega_parse_source` answers with. So does a source the parser refuses — one it answers with a `halt` diagnostic beside its tree: the importer's call fails with the message of each such diagnostic, in the parser's order, and is never handed the tree. Called directly with `aggrega plugin run-local --export parse`, a parser is handed the authored JSON payload converted into this encoding — the source written in that payload as base64, as JSON writes any byte field — and its answer is read as the export's output shape and printed as JSON — an answer that is not that shape is refused, naming the export, as a build refuses it.

A client opens a session over that daemon with the handshake, and the session is what scopes the settings and the workspace the conversation was opened over; the daemon is the process that answers a request, sends a notification and holds what it has read. The protocol is JSON-RPC 2.0 over standard input and output, each message framed by a Content-Length header; this document describes the message bodies and neither the framing nor the transport. A body is one of four things: a request the client sends, a notification the client sends, a notification the daemon sends, or the response the daemon returns for a request. Three properties of the surface decide how the shapes below are written. First, every request admits two fields beyond the ones its own method declares — `workspaceRoot`, naming the workspace the request acts on, and `workDoneToken`, the caller-minted value progress is reported under — so both appear on every request params object here, including the three methods whose subject is not a workspace and which accept `workspaceRoot` and ignore it. Second, the daemon refuses a request params object carrying a field the method does not accept, naming what it does accept, so every params object here is closed at its top level; a nested object inside a request is not closed, because the check reads only the outermost field names. Third, a result is composed by the daemon rather than supplied by a caller, so result objects are closed at every level whose shape is fixed, and open only where the value is opaque JSON the daemon carries through without reading. One consequence of the daemon's encoding is visible on the wire and is described rather than tidied away: a collection the daemon does not mark optional is emitted as `null` when it has no value to report and as an empty collection when the value it reports is empty, so both forms are admitted wherever that applies.

8ee59b5358e362dd: `metadata.labels`: Use `feature.aggrega.ai/kind: secret` to mark a Feature as a credential Feature. The label is descriptive metadata for the author, for the catalog site, and for label selectors; no compiler branch reads it, and what an attachment produces is decided by the FeatureRecipe the Manifest maps its type to, not by the label. A credential Feature and an ordinary Feature are attached the same way, on the same attachment surface, at any scope. The standard library's credential family splits by *result*: **`core/secret-value`** delivers a value into the inject pipe; **`core/referenced-secret`** names a referenceable secret resource (a Kubernetes Secret, an AWS Secrets Manager secret, a Vault entry), one its FeatureRecipe's output creates or one that already exists, and declares a `schema.provides` output contract — `name` (the resource's provider-neutral locator) and `key` (the data field within it) — that a consumer reads as `.features.<slot>.provides.<key>` to reference the resource without re-deriving its name; **`core/referenced-secret-set`** materializes one resource carrying a caller-supplied set of data keys and publishes the locator alone, for a consumer whose target already knows the key names it reads; **`core/secret-provided`** exposes a pre-existing secret's value; **`core/generated-secret`** produces nothing, because the target engine generates and manages the credential itself, so it declares neither `values` nor `provides` and its FeatureRecipes are pure wiring that render no bytes. Two axes separate the members: who supplies the material — an author writes it or names where to fetch it, or the target engine owns it outright, as with `core/generated-secret` — and what the attachment yields, an injected value or a referenceable resource or nothing rendered at all. Every member is a peer of the others on the same attachment surface, so a credential slot is always bound and what varies between Releases is what binds it. A credential Feature that declares a `schema.provides` contract obliges every FeatureRecipe implementing it to publish those keys — the build halts otherwise — and a `featuresSchema` slot's `selector` targets the family member it needs.

8f072b5eaf0a556a: A registry that is too busy answers 429 Too Many Requests, or 503 Service Unavailable with a `Retry-After` header saying how long to wait. Every request a command makes to a registry waits as long as the registry asks — ten seconds where it does not say — and is asked again; every request to that registry waits with it, and fewer are sent to it at once until it answers again. A registry that answers nothing but "slow down" for five minutes is refused under this condition, naming the registry, its last answer and how long it had answered nothing else, and so is a request whose own time limit ends while it waits. `aggrega registry update` then reports that registry as not indexed, and it keeps the index it had before the run.

Canonical means identical input produces identical bytes on every side, which is what lets a payload be compared across the three plugin kits rather than only round-tripped, and it is why a build's output stays byte-identical. A guest reads and writes it through the entry points its kit's payload type already carries — `DecodeCBOR` and `EncodeCBOR` in Go, `decode_cbor` and `encode_cbor` in Rust, `decodeCBORMutatorInput` and `encodeCBORMutatorOutput` in TypeScript — so no CBOR library is needed and nothing hand-parses bytes. In Rust the export takes and returns `Vec<u8>`; in TypeScript it reads `Host.inputBytes()` and writes `Host.outputBytes(...)`. The graph's `nodes`, and each node's `labels`, are maps the schema marks order-preserving, so they cross as [ordered lists of entries](#maps-that-keep-their-order) — the nodes in the order the build holds them, which is author order, and each node's labels in the order the node carries them — and a guest reads both through its kit's order-keeping container.

**Centralized Enterprise Governance (Evaluating Complete Reality):**
Relying on out-of-band mechanisms (like `CODEOWNERS` on a git repository) to govern architecture is a weak workaround. All governance is localized in the compiler's governance verdict roles. Because the AOT compiler builds the IR Graph by flattening *both* the Developer's `Aggregate` and the Ops Engineer's `Release`, the policy engine evaluates the complete reality before physical artifacts are generated. Policies can fatally halt the build if a developer requests an unapproved Component, if Ops maps a component to an unapproved Recipe in the Manifest, or if an insecure Wasm mutation is attached to a Component carrying a `restricted` subsystem label.
91d5cc1ce607e467: **An alignment reports whether it changed anything, and that is the field to act on.** `changed` separates a write from an alignment that found the records already correct: an unchanged file was left byte-identical, so a client holding that document has nothing to reload, and running the request twice reports no change the second time. `entity` names the file, `hostFunctions` carries the derived set, and `commands` carries the mirror as values rather than as the line a terminal prints — each entry a `name`, an optional `description`, and `flags`, each flag carrying its `name` and its optional `shorthand`, `description`, `type` and `default`. The write is atomic, so a client reading that file while the alignment runs never observes a partial document.

91d608780ef9bf3f: Because the Aggrega compiler is mathematically unopinionated, it possesses zero hardcoded knowledge of AI frameworks, token budgets, or memory partitioning. Instead, the generic cloud-native schemas act as an empty vessel. Rather than being hardcoded into the compiler core, highly specialized domain intelligence is distributed across the entire extensible Aggrega ecosystem. It is encapsulated within the Platform Catalog through specialized `components`, `features`, and `recipes`. Developers preserve their specific application intent within their `values` and `uses` blocks — strictly governed by the Architect's `schema:` declarations (compact form or full JSON Schema 2020-12) — while the physical translation of that intelligence is executed by target-specific WebAssembly plugins.

925a286772cae701: **Resilience:** `core/fallback-chain` sends a request whose model fails on to other models: `chains` names, for each model alias that falls back, the aliases to try in order until one answers, a fallback that fails following its own entry in turn, and `max_hops` bounds how far along that chain a request is passed. The standard library realizes it on the AI gateway by writing both into the routing configuration the gateway's Recipe renders, and halts the build on a name the gateway's model map does not publish. A request falls back only once the gateway has given up on the alias it asked for: where one alias is published more than once, a failed call first moves to another of its entries as a retry, bounded by the gateway's retry count. `core/retry-policy` sets that count — how many times the gateway may send a request, the first send included (`max_attempts`), for a failure that succeeds on being sent again, such as a refused connection, a rate limit or a timeout — and the standard library realizes it on the AI gateway by writing it into the routing configuration the gateway's Recipe renders. On `core/gateway/envoy-gateway` it is realized as the retry of the traffic policy on the route serving the wired models, the same policy that carries a period budget's rate limit, because Envoy Gateway attaches one traffic policy to a route: a request is sent again after a refused connection or stream, a reset or a reply of 429, 503 or 504, up to `max_attempts` sends, and a model that answers nothing within the route's request timeout is not sent again, because that timeout spans every send. On `core/gateway/azure-api-management` it is realized as Azure's retry around the forwarding, in the backend section of the API's policy: a request answered with HTTP 429 or a 5xx status is sent again, its body held so it can be resent, one second after the previous send, up to `max_attempts` sends. A refused or dropped connection, and a model that answers nothing within the forwarding's timeout, are not sent again, because Azure ends the retry on such an error and hands it to the policy's on-error section. Azure retries 1 to 50 times after the first send, so a `max_attempts` of 1 writes no retry and one above 51 is refused by name. The retry takes the place of the forwarding the API would inherit, so while it is attached a forwarding setting made at a broader scope of the instance, such as a timeout, does not apply to the API, which forwards with Azure's defaults. On the hosted gateway, `core/retry-policy` is realized by writing into the gateway's resource its retry count, which names the sends after the first, from 1 to 5, so `max_attempts` from 2 to 6 is honoured and any other value refused; `core/fallback-chain` is not realized there, because that gateway falls back between models only inside a route a request names in place of a model, so a request for a model never falls back. On `core/gateway/kong-enterprise`, `core/fallback-chain` is realized on its chart Recipe: the chat and completion routes of each alias `chains` gives an entry carry Kong's AI Proxy Advanced in place of its AI proxy, with the alias's model and the models its walk falls back to as targets in priority order — the alias, then its entry's fallbacks in order, a fallback's own entry followed in turn only while fewer than `max_hops` have been counted. The balancer sends a request to each target of the walk once, in order, until one answers, moving on after a connection error or timeout, an invalid reply header or a reply of 429, 500, 502, 503 or 504, and returns every other reply as it came. The build halts on a name the `models` socket does not carry, on a walk reaching an alias twice, beside `core/retry-policy`, since Kong keeps one retry count for the whole walk and cannot send to a model again before falling back, and on a gateway image older than 3.12. `core/retry-policy` is not realized there, and its realization halts every attachment naming why: each wired model is served on routes of its own carrying that one model, so a retry has to send the request to that same target again, and Kong's reference reads both ways on whether its balancer does. On `core/gateway/agentgateway`, `core/retry-policy` is realized on the chart Recipe as a retry policy of the gateway's own configuration, attached to the listener its model requests arrive on: a request is sent again, at once and to the same model, after a reply of 429, 500, 502, 503 or 504, a refused or reset connection, a connection taking longer than 11 seconds to open or a failed name lookup, up to `max_attempts` sends. agentgateway sends a request once more than its policy's attempts, so the policy is written as `max_attempts` less one, `max_attempts` 1 writes none, and one above 256 is refused by name. A request whose body is larger than 64 KiB is sent once, and the configuration sets no timeout, so a model that accepts the connection and answers nothing is waited on rather than sent again. `core/fallback-chain` is not realized there, and its realization halts every attachment naming why: agentgateway fails over between models by evicting a failed one for the requests after it, while the request that failed is answered with its failure, so no request is walked along a chain. On `core/gateway/higress`, `core/retry-policy` is realized as the route's own retry, written as Ingress annotations onto every model route: a request is sent again after a refused or reset connection, a 5xx reply or a 429, a POST included, up to `max_attempts` sends; `max_attempts` 1 writes the retry off, overriding the retry Higress's control plane gives a route carrying no annotation, and one above 2147483648 is refused by name. A model that accepts the connection and then answers nothing or slowly is not sent again, since the route sets no per-try deadline, and a streamed request is sent again only before its reply has begun. `core/fallback-chain` is not realized there either, and its realization halts every attachment naming why: Higress sends a failed request on at most once, to one other destination — a route's default backend, or the one fallback route its console writes for an AI route — so no request is walked along a chain. On `core/gateway/traefik-hub` both are realized on the chart Recipe, and each halts the build on a Traefik Hub image older than v3.20, whose failover takes no middlewares on the services it tries and whose retry cannot send a POST again on a reply's status — a retry policy of one send excepted. `core/fallback-chain` sends the route of each alias `chains` gives an entry through nested failovers of Traefik's own, trying the models of the alias's walk in order — the alias, then its entry's fallbacks in order, a fallback's own entry followed in turn only while fewer than `max_hops` have been counted — each with its own model name, credential, quotas and retry. A model's reply of 429 or of 500 to 504, after any retry of that model, moves the request on to the next; any other reply is returned as it came, the last model's whatever it is, and a request body over 1 MiB is refused with HTTP 413 rather than sent. The build halts on a name the `models` socket does not carry and on a walk reaching an alias twice. `core/retry-policy` is Traefik's retry middleware, last on each model route, or on each model a walk tries: a request is sent again at once after a connection that carried nothing to the model and after a reply of 429 or of 500 to 504, a POST included, up to `max_attempts` sends, the first included, and `max_attempts` 1 writes nothing. A reply the gateway forms itself — a refusal of its key check, a guard, the masking or a quota — is never sent again, and neither is a streamed reply once it has begun.

That is the shape a fill meant for the slot takes when it is written under the wrong name: left alone it would be a free attachment while the slot stays empty, and an optional slot left empty builds green and delivers nothing. The message names the attachment, the component, the Feature and each empty slot that Feature fits, and the remedy is to attach it under the slot's name. It holds for every Feature, not only for credentials. Everything else on the surface stays free: an attachment whose Feature fits no declared slot, an extra attachment once every slot it fits is bound, and an attachment the component inherits from a subsystem or a Release boundary — so the shared shape above is untouched. A slot declaring no `selector` says nothing about which Feature it is for, so no attachment is held to it this way. The halt is described in [errors/fatal-halts.md](../errors/fatal-halts.md) under "An attachment written under another name fits a slot its component leaves empty".

9283eba1ed8b09d3: Optional per-boundary deployment wave (signed integer, default 0). Every component in this boundary inherits the boundary's wave into its node. Negative values are permitted (run before everything else); larger values run after lower ones. On K8s and Helm the wave is what orders the deployment: it becomes an `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave` annotation, and on a resource the chart already marks as a Helm hook it also becomes that hook's `helm.sh/hook-weight`. On compose the wave both is recorded as a service label and orders the services of the file it renders into, through `depends_on` between them — so it reaches every service in that one file and nothing outside it. On cloudformation the wave orders provisioning of the stack the boundary assembles into: every resource in a wave is declared to depend on the resources of the wave before it, which fixes the order they are created in and, in reverse, the order they are deleted in. That is creation and deletion order only — a stack template expresses no notion of a resource being ready, so nothing waits for one to become serviceable. On terraform the wave orders the module blocks of the root configuration the boundary assembles into: every module in a wave is declared to depend on the modules of the wave before it, which fixes the order the engine performs its actions in. That is action order only — a configuration expresses no notion of a resource being ready, so nothing waits for one to become serviceable — and the value is also recorded with the node's build provenance. The compiler carries the same value onto every node in the boundary as that node's `sync_wave`, where the per-target behaviour is described again from the node's side. Nested boundaries do not implicitly inherit — each declares its own wave.
92872b20db7f2b5e: Each entry's template evaluates against the self-contained provides-evaluation surface — `.context.instance_id`, `.context.rendered_name` where the node's provider reports one, `.values`, `.infra`, the node's resolved `.locals`, and static text. The namespace the node is placed in is not on it, so a published host carries none: a consumer in another namespace qualifies it on its own side. `.locals` is on it because the node's locals resolve in the preamble of the same stage, ahead of its provides; a `provides` template naming a key the locals block does not declare halts. Callers then read these values via `.context.uses.<alias>.provides.<provided-name>` in their own templates — the provided names nest under `provides` on the edge, alongside the edge's other fields. A caller that declares an `inject:` allowlist on the edge reaches the same values through its `.context.inject` pipe instead.

Every size these operations report is written in the same vocabulary that cap is read in, so a figure you read off a cache report is one you can type straight into the cap prompt. A cap the compiler cannot read comes back with the compiler's own message naming what a size cap looks like. Cleared and trimmed caches repopulate on the next build that needs them. Each entry binds one provider capability (the bare capability name a Recipe binds through `spec.capability`, e.g. `helm` or `compose`) to the bare identity of the provider-rendering plugin that serves it (the Plugin entity's identity, its `metadata.pluginType` and `metadata.name` joined by a slash, e.g. `provider/helm`), with an optional trailing `:version` in the same three forms as a version pin (bare, exact `:1.0.0`, or major-compatible range `:^1.0.0`). This is the disambiguation and override surface for a federated catalog where more than one provider plugin serves the same capability: the binding selects which publisher's plugin renders that capability. When a capability is served by exactly one provider plugin no entry is needed. Exactly one entry per capability is permitted across the composed list; a duplicate capability halts resolution loudly. Resolution is at pull: the pull records the resolved binding into the per-Release lockfile, and the build reads the lockfile — a change here after a pull is not adopted until the next pull, so build output is invariant to it (deterministic output). Every build and every validation of a Release also checks each entry here, whether or not a Recipe asks for its capability: an entry naming a plugin the build holds that does not serve the entry's capability halts, naming what that plugin serves and a spelling one edit away when there is one; an entry naming a capability and no plugin, where no provider plugin the build reads serves that capability, is reported as a warning rather than halting, because the plugin serving it may be one only another Release reads; and an entry for a capability a plugin serves but this Release never asks for is legal and reported as nothing, since entries are written for the whole workspace and a build is of one Release. A `capability` containing a colon is refused when the configuration loads: a Recipe's `spec.capability` is read as the capability up to its last colon and a version pin after it, so no Recipe could reach such an entry. A missing entry for an unambiguously-served capability is not an error; a missing entry for an ambiguously-served capability halts the pull loudly, listing the candidate plugins. Version coexistence is preserved: the binding selects the plugin repository per capability, and each Recipe's own `spec.capability` version pin selects the version within that repository, so two Recipes pinning different versions of one provider still coexist. 9a089413ed690a9a: **Send `sync` to bring what an earlier import drafted up to date with the source instead**, changing only what the import wrote. A sync sent no `target` drafts for the target the record names, so it drafts the Manifest the earlier import drafted; one sent a `target` drafts for it, and the record then names it. A recorded target no Recipe in the catalog binds to is refused as a sent one is, the refusal saying the target is the recorded one. Each part is judged three ways — what the record says the import last wrote there, what is on disk, and what the source drafts now. A part the source left as the import last wrote it stays exactly as it is on disk, whether or not an author edited it. A part the source changed is written anew, a part it dropped is removed — a drafted file deleted whole — and a part it gained is added beside the parts the draft names around it, each only where what is on disk is what the import last wrote and holds nothing an author added. Everything else stays byte for byte: a key an author added anywhere — a parameter, a Feature, under a drafted Component instance too, another Component, the environment a drafted Release leaves for its author — a comment not written directly above a drafted key, and every file the record does not list. The answer's `drift` lists each part brought up to date — or, under `dry_run`, each part that would be — in the order the draft names them, each as `change` (`added`, `removed` or `changed`), `file`, the drafted file it is in, and `key`, the keys leading to it in a drafted Aggregate or Release as a list, empty where the part is the whole file; the text answer names each on a line of its own in the words `aggrega import` writes on standard error, `<change> <key> in <file>` or `<change> <file>`. An empty `drift` under `dry_run` says the drafts are in step with the source. Under `dry_run` the drafts handed back are the files the sync would write, with the content it would give them. **A sync that would change or remove a part an author edited, add a part where an author already wrote one, or remove a part holding something an author added is refused**, naming each such part and why, and nothing is written; a comment written directly above a drafted key edits that key. A sync over an Aggregate no record lists is refused saying so, as is one whose record cannot be read, and a sync whose importer could not finish writes nothing. A sync into a directory holding no record and nothing at its drafted paths writes the whole draft. `drift` is an empty list for a call that is not a sync.

**Action:** The CLI fetches all requested entities (Components, Features, Releases). It first checks these definitions for the `extends` keyword. 9c690d27b01386f7:
**The Deterministic Output Rule (GitOps Safety):**
Because GitOps controllers (ArgoCD, Flux) perform byte-level diff detection on rendered artifacts, the compiler guarantees that identical inputs produce byte-identical outputs. Maps that flow through the template context (`.context.inject.env`, `.values`, `.infra`, and the rest of the runtime view) are backed by ordered-map structures that preserve author insertion order across the data layer, and the template boundary is the one exception: `{{ range }}` over those maps iterates in alphabetical key order, as Go templates do, not in author order. Ops engineers can rely on that iteration order being deterministic across runs of the same input; where sequence carries meaning, it is authored as a list rather than recovered from a map. The Sprig `keys` function, however, returns Go-map iteration order (which is non-deterministic by language design); templates that compose a deterministic key sequence from `keys` output must pipe through `sortAlpha` (e.g., `{{ keys .values | sortAlpha }}`) to recover determinism.

**The schema-bridge pattern for infrastructure-aware components.**
The Component exposes the specific infrastructure dial inside the developer's `values` block through its `schema:` declaration, and the bound Recipe's `valuesMapping:` template pipes the value into the rendered `infra:`-shaped output. The result is a typed bridge between cognitive intent and physical sizing: the developer dictates the hardware constraint through a validated field, and the constraint flows to Ops without either side writing raw infrastructure code. The dial is a pillar key, so it is declared on the Component whose contract owns it — a Component that `extends:` a base declares no pillar keys and therefore cannot introduce one.

The Deployment and StatefulSet carry the replica count; DaemonSet, Job, and CronJob carry none. A `stateful` Workload requires exactly one `type: Headless` Service declared in the Workload to govern the StatefulSet; the provider wires the StatefulSet's `serviceName` to that Service's rendered name, and the build halts if no headless Service is declared (or if more than one is). a06ce6c3b3e0dac3: **Where the workspace names no catalog folder, the import reads the catalog its default registry publishes.** A workspace whose `workspace.catalog_dirs`, `AGGREGA_CATALOG_DIRS` and root name no catalog folder reads the standard-library catalog as one signed snapshot, at `catalog/snapshot` on its default registry. A snapshot is fetched once: its signature is verified under that registry's trust policy, and it is kept in the workspace's content cache and read there as a catalog folder, held to its digest, with no registry asked for it again. Which snapshot a request reads: with `upgrade`, the newest; otherwise the one the record in `outputDir` names, fetched by its digest where the machine does not hold it; otherwise the one the workspace last fetched as the newest; otherwise the newest. The record the import writes names the snapshot it read, by its digest, so a later request into the same `outputDir` reads the same catalog. Under the offline posture a request that would have to fetch a snapshot is an error under [The workspace is offline and the step needs the network](../errors/fatal-halts.md#the-workspace-is-offline-and-the-step-needs-the-network), naming what to run, and `upgrade` is refused whatever the machine holds, since only the registry can say which snapshot is the newest. A registry that publishes no snapshot leaves the import with no catalog, and a `warn` entry in `diagnostics` says so. a07a423c012e27ce:
**Directories listed under `workspace.catalog_dirs` are read as well, and they are read first.**
The list is an ordered search stack: the first directory to declare an identity owns it, and the
same identity in a later directory is shadowed. A library name (SchemaLibrary, MappingLibrary, WorkloadLibrary, ArtifactLibrary) is owned as a whole: the first directory that holds any version of it owns it, and every copy in a later directory, at any version, is shadowed. `catalog` is read after everything listed — unless
a listed directory already contains it, in which case it is read as part of that directory — so
listing a directory adds to what you had rather than replacing it. A repeatable `--catalog <dir>`
on the command line is read ahead of both, and a relative path given there resolves against the
directory you ran the command from, since no configuration file declared it. A directory named more
than once — on the command line and in the list, or twice in the list — is read once, at the place it
was first named, so nothing in it is reported as shadowed by itself: a shadow is always two different
files declaring one identity. Two spellings of one directory, a path to it through a link, and — on a
file system that ignores case — a spelling in another case all name that one directory. A directory
inside another listed directory is still read as its own entry. A project that keeps a
catalog variant per Release can give each Release a list of its own instead — see
[Giving a Release its own catalog directories](#giving-a-release-its-own-catalog-directories).

A guest decodes its input and encodes its output through the entry points its kit's `ImportInput` and `ImportOutput` already carry — `DecodeCBOR` and `EncodeCBOR` in Go, `decode_cbor` and `encode_cbor` in Rust, `decodeCBORImportInput` and `encodeCBORImportOutput` in TypeScript — reading and writing bytes (`Vec<u8>` in Rust, `Host.inputBytes()` and `Host.outputBytes(...)` in TypeScript). No CBOR library is needed and nothing hand-parses bytes. `settings` crosses inside the binary document as the bytes of its JSON document, so a guest parses it as JSON to look inside, as on every other socket. An importer that cannot complete says why in the output's `error`, and the import halts naming the importer and that message; an answer that is not an `ImportOutput` in this encoding — one written as JSON, or one carrying a top-level field the shape does not declare — halts the import too, naming the importer and its `import` export. a6e4de34151fb189: **Period budget:** `core/period-budget` bounds what the traffic through a gateway may consume over a period: a `limit`, the `period` it covers, a `scope` — everything the gateway serves, each caller or each model — and a `unit` — a cost in US dollars or tokens — and once what the gateway has counted over the period exceeds the limit, further model requests are refused. It attaches to any component declaring `dataplane.aggrega.ai/period-budget`. The standard library realizes it on the AI gateway, whose budget covers everything the gateway serves, is counted in US dollars, and starts again at the start of every period — a number of days from midnight UTC, or a calendar month from its first day: the realization writes the limit and the period into the configuration the gateway's Recipe renders, refuses any other unit, scope or period by name — `30d` among them, which the gateway counts as a calendar month — and halts unless the gateway's `database_url` and `api_key` credential slots are both attached, because without its bookkeeping database the gateway keeps no count and without an administrative key it checks no caller against the budget. Once the count exceeds the limit, the gateway refuses the administrative key's model requests as well as every caller's; its model listing and key management still answer that key. On the hosted gateway it is realized as a spend-limit rule on the gateway's resource, counted in US dollars over a window that moves forward with time — the last `period`, for models whose pricing the gateway knows — for everything the gateway serves: a budget per caller or per model, tokens and a calendar month are refused by name. APISIX counts no tokens on a completion request, so while the budget is attached each wired model gets its chat route alone, and it keeps the count in the memory of the gateway process, so the chart runs one replica and a restart opens a new window. Once the count exceeds the limit the gateway answers model requests with HTTP 429 until the window ends; a request's tokens are added once its reply completes, so the request that crosses the limit is served. a72a090c78ef8359: The Aggrega compiler relies on a strictly typed, OAM-inspired registry to resolve abstract Developer Intent (Domain 1) into concrete Ops Reality (Domain 3). To support an open, distributed ecosystem while maintaining a seamless developer experience, all schemas, infrastructure bindings, programmable policies, and adapter plugins follow a standardized Open Container Initiative (OCI) URI taxonomy. **`render-verdict`** — the guest reasons over the rendered output, after
  rendering. The payload carries the emitted artifacts sorted by path, so the wire
  is byte-identical across runs of identical input. Each artifact carries its
  output path and its rendered text; it additionally carries the format it was
  rendered in, when the producing provider declared one, and a parsed structured
  view of its content, when the content is in a format that was parsed ahead of the
  policy. A `render-verdict` policy sees exactly what the build produced, and
  nothing in it is withheld: a value a Recipe rendered into an artifact arrives
  as rendered, because the artifact is what the policy judges. Use it
  for policies about the concrete output — a rule that inspects rendered Docker
  Compose services or Kubernetes objects, for example.
aa0d4bdb67cbd9f0: **Semantic caching:** `core/semantic-caching` declares a cache that answers a prompt with the reply stored for an earlier one close enough in meaning, rather than calling the model again. `embedding_model` names the model that turns each prompt into a vector, as the gateway publishes it, a stored reply is served when the two prompts are at least `similarity_threshold` alike, and it stays usable for `ttl_seconds`. `scope` decides who shares a cache: `end_user`, the default, keeps each end user the gateway identifies apart, while `key` serves every caller presenting one key from one cache, so an end user behind that key can be served a reply generated for another. It does not meet `core/data-masking` on one component. The standard library realizes it on the AI gateway, which keeps the replies in a `core/datastore/redis` wired to its `cache_store` socket, presenting to the store the password the credential on that connection holds where the store requires one, the store removing each reply once `ttl_seconds` have passed, and caches chat, responses and messages requests, not completions or embeddings. The realization halts the build unless the gateway's `api_key` slot is attached, because without an administrative key the gateway checks no caller, on an `embedding_model` the gateway's model map does not publish, and when nothing is wired to `cache_store`. A stored reply is served only to a request matching what it was stored under: the key the request presents, which the gateway verifies, with that key's team and organization; under `end_user`, the end user the request names; and the model the request asks for with its other parameters. The gateway writes the key, team, organization and end user into the request itself, over any value a caller sent for them on a chat request; on a responses or messages request it removes a team, organization or end user field from the request's own metadata and refuses one naming the key there, so no request can name its way into another key's replies. A request's own metadata can still move it among the replies of the key it presents: on a responses request `model_group` replaces the model it asks for in what its reply is stored under; on a responses or messages request `caching_groups` lets requests naming the same group of model aliases share replies across them; and on a responses or chat request `redis_namespace` keeps requests naming a namespace apart from those naming none. The gateway reads an end user from a header or a body field the request itself names, and verifies none of them: under `end_user` a caller naming another end user is served that end user's replies, and requests naming no end user share one cache with every other such request under the key they present. The hosted gateway does not realize it: its cache answers only a request identical to an earlier one. On `core/gateway/azure-api-management` it is realized as Azure's semantic cache lookup and store, written into the API's policy: `embedding_model` names a backend the API Management instance already holds for an embeddings model, which the instance reaches with its managed identity, and the instance needs a Redis cache with RediSearch configured as its external cache, neither of which the build can see, so the build halts until the operator affirms that the cache serves RediSearch by setting the gateway's `infra.cache_serves_vector_search`; the store keeps a reply for `ttl_seconds`; and `similarity_threshold` is written as Azure's score threshold, one minus the threshold, reading that score as a cosine distance, since Microsoft gives its range and its direction — lower requires closer prompts — but not its measure. A reply is stored and served apart per API and per API Management subscription, whose key the gateway verifies, so the realization keeps `key`, refuses it on an API that requires no subscription key, and refuses `end_user`: the API its Recipe renders validates no end user's token, so the gateway has no verified end user to keep apart. Nor do `core/gateway/contour` and `core/gateway/nginx`, which offer no semantic cache. On `core/gateway/agentgateway` its realization halts every attachment, naming why: agentgateway keeps no cache of replies, and its prompt caching only marks where a provider that caches prompts itself may do so. On `core/gateway/kong-enterprise` its realization halts every attachment, naming the scope asked for: Kong's AI Semantic Cache has no setting that keeps one caller's stored replies apart from another's, and the gateway tells callers apart only as the consumers an authentication plugin names and declares no callers, for the reasons "Kong in front of models" above gives, so under `end_user` and under `key` alike every request would share one cache. On `core/gateway/higress` its realization halts every attachment, naming the scope asked for: Higress's semantic cache stores each reply under one key prefix followed by the prompt text, and nothing in that key names a caller or an end user, while the gateway declares no callers, so every request would share one cache. On `core/gateway/apisix` it is realized on the chart Recipe, written onto each wired model's chat route as APISIX 3.18.0's semantic cache, for the callers its Release declares in `infra.callers`: a reply is stored per route and per caller, under the key the caller presented, which the gateway verifies, so no caller is served a reply stored for another; the realization keeps `key` and refuses `end_user` by name, because the gateway cannot tell apart the end users behind one key. `embedding_model` names a connection on the gateway's `models` socket, whose endpoint, model and credential the cache embeds with. The cache embeds a request's last user message and serves a stored reply whose message is at least `similarity_threshold` alike and whose earlier messages — a system prompt, earlier turns — are the same. The replies sit for `ttl_seconds` in a `core/datastore/redis` wired to the gateway's `cache_store` socket, to which the cache presents the password the credential on that connection holds, and a reply served by meaning is stored again under that request for `ttl_seconds` more. Completion requests are not cached, and a store or embedding failure is a miss: the request is still answered. The realization halts with no caller declared, with nothing wired to `cache_store` or to the `models` socket, and on an `embedding_model` no connection there carries. APISIX keys a stored reply by route and caller rather than by gateway, so two APISIX gateways wired to one store, or two Releases of one Aggregate pointing their gateway at one external store, can serve a cached reply to a caller of the same name on the same alias and model. Its workload Recipe, at APISIX 3.17.0, carries no semantic cache at all. On `core/gateway/traefik-hub` it is realized on the chart Recipe as Traefik Hub's semantic cache on the route of each wired model, for the callers its Release declares in `infra.callers`: a reply is stored per wired model and per caller, under the caller the gateway's key check verified, each by its own key, so no caller is served a reply stored for another; the realization keeps `key` and refuses `end_user` by name, because the gateway cannot tell apart the end users behind one key. `embedding_model` names a connection on the gateway's `models` socket, whose endpoint, model and credential the cache embeds a request's text with. `similarity_threshold` is written as the cache's distance bound, one minus the threshold, read as a cosine distance, since Traefik's reference gives the bound's direction but not its measure. A reply is kept for `ttl_seconds` in a `core/datastore/redis` wired to the gateway's `cache_store` socket, and a request too large to embed is answered uncached. The realization halts with no caller declared, with nothing wired to `cache_store` or to the `models` socket, on an `embedding_model` no connection there carries, and on a Traefik Hub image whose tag names no release from v3.19.11 within 3.19 or from v3.20.6, since an earlier release shares one cache among every caller of a route.
aa0e0bef043628c2: 🔴 **`halted: true` is not an error, and treating it as one is the mistake to design against.** An importer that could not convert everything still drafts what it could: the response carries those drafts, `written` names them, and `diagnostics` says what was left out. That is the most useful answer the operation gives, and it arrives as a result rather than as a failure precisely so you can show the author both halves. Under `sync` the same answer writes nothing — `files`, `written` and `drift` are empty — because a partial draft would read as a source that dropped every part the importer did not reach. A source the importer could not read at all is a different case and does come back as an error.

aa8577b27444db8e: **The host runtime: a capability-denying sandbox.** Aggrega embeds the Wasm host as the Extism toolkit running on top of the Wazero engine; the host binary stays pure Go with no native toolchain dependency, so `aggrega` cross-compiles cleanly. Every socket runs behind an **AOT-purity firewall**: the host refuses to grant a plugin any runtime-access capability — no network, no filesystem, no wall-clock, no environment, no standard I/O — so a call that would use one fails, and a plugin importing from a host surface the host does not provide is rejected at load. A plugin that cannot reach the network or read the clock cannot break the compiler's ahead-of-time guarantee that the same input produces the same output. Language runtimes that need a few benign startup imports run against a capability-denied configuration of those imports: the host fixes the observable wall clock, supplies real entropy, discards standard I/O, and grants no filesystem, argument, or environment access — so a plugin can reach no host capability that varies across builds. Entropy is deliberately left real rather than pinned: pinning it would stabilise a guest language runtime's internal hash seed and map-iteration order, and so hide a plugin whose own output is not reproducible instead of letting that surface as differing output. A plugin whose result depends on entropy is an authoring-level determinism problem, and this configuration is built to reveal it rather than mask it.

adefa700b3acef1e: **A catalog entity named with a Release is checked as a single entity, in that Release's terms.** A `file` holding a Component, a Feature, a Recipe, a FeatureRecipe or a Plugin, sent with a `release`, gets the check [`aggrega validate <path> --release <release>`](aggrega-validate.md#checking-an-entity-in-a-releases-terms) runs, over the editor's unsaved buffer: its references — the Component a Recipe implements, a library a pillar refers to — resolve through the catalog directories the workspace configuration gives that Release, so one file can be clean in the terms of the Release that builds with it and fail in the terms of a Release whose directories do not hold what it refers to. That is the verdict the command line and the `validate` tool of [`aggrega mcp`](aggrega-mcp.md) give for the same entity beside the same Release, and like theirs it walks no closure and reads no lockfile. A blocking finding is one error entry in the check's own words and carrying its codes, drawn on the key it names in the entity and, where it names none, on the entity's `kind:` key, as [What a diagnostic entry carries](#what-a-diagnostic-entry-carries) describes — unless a build already reports that fault on the file, in which case the build's entry is the one report; an advisory the check raises while reading the catalog is a warning entry ahead of it; a clean check over directories that are all there answers no entry. A failed assertion — one that calls `fail`, in the Recipe or in the Component it implements — is not a blocking finding here but a warning entry, in the check's words and carrying its codes, closed by the sentence `A Release must satisfy this assertion before a build of it can pass.`, and drawn where the blocking finding would be: a Recipe's assertion on that assertion's own key under `assertions`, a Component's on the Recipe's `kind:` key. Like a blocking finding, it gives way to a build's entry reporting the same fault on the file. The check builds the entity around placeholders and schema defaults rather than the values a Release sets, so it cannot tell an assertion waiting on a Release from one that is broken, and leaves the verdict to a build, which reports the same assertion as an error ([a failed assertion is a warning](aggrega-validate.md#a-failed-assertion-is-a-warning)). A directory the workspace configuration lists for the Release that is not a directory — nothing exists there, say — is not checked past: the file carries one error entry instead of the check's verdict, the refusal every command gives that directory, naming the entry, the configuration file and line listing it and the setting ([Where local entities are read from](configuration.md#where-local-entities-are-read-from)). A `release` naming no file, or naming a directory, is answered on the file with the sentence the command line refuses it with, rather than checked in the workspace's terms. What a build of one cannot stand in for is judged as the command line judges it, and what the command line sets aside or does not check answers no entry here — see [what single-entity correctness does not check](aggrega-validate.md#what-single-entity-correctness-does-not-check), and, for a Recipe whose template reads a value only a topology edge or an attached credential delivers, [single-entity correctness](aggrega-validate.md#single-entity-correctness-an-entity-path). The Release's own Aggregate, a Manifest, a Release and a library are not checked one at a time, because the single-entity check does not take those kinds; they keep the closure's checks above. A buffer holding Workload content is read as YAML that is not an Aggrega document, because that content is written inside a Recipe's or a FeatureRecipe's `workload:` field and is checked there, where it sits; the command line and the `validate` tool, handed a Workload file by path, check its shape on its own.

af3875f68c4c97da: Default OCI registry entities are published to and dependencies are resolved from when an entity does not name a registry explicitly: `aggrega push` publishes there and `aggrega pull` fetches from there. Defaults to `hub.aggrega.ai`. Write the `name` of an entry under `registries`, which then stands for that entry's `host`; the host itself; or the host followed by `/` and a repository path, such as `ghcr.io/acme` or `harbor.example.com/platform`. A name is matched first: a value that is the `name` of one entry is that entry's host, even where it is also spelled like a host, so publishing, pulling, signature verification and every per-registry trust setting use that one host; a value two entries are named after is refused as ambiguous, and a name followed by a path is refused, because a name stands for an entry's host and not for a location under it. Any other value must be a host, written in the spelling its trust policy is kept under: a lowercase host name containing a dot (`registry.example.com`), `localhost`, a single name followed by a port (`registry:5000`), an IPv4 address, or an IPv6 address in brackets (`[::1]`), each with an optional `:port` and with no scheme, credentials, whitespace or capital letter — optionally followed by a repository path: one or more segments of lowercase letters and digits joined by `/`, which may be separated inside a segment by `.`, `_`, `__` or dashes, with no tag, digest or trailing `/`. The path is where things are published and fetched: every entity published through the default registry is published under `<host>/<path>/`, and every entity resolved through it is fetched from there, so what one publishes the other finds. It is never part of how a registry is trusted: the `registries` entry whose policy applies, a login, a signing requirement and the trusted identities are all found by the host alone. Port 443 on a host reached over HTTPS is that host's default port, and writing it is refused, naming the spelling to write without it; `localhost` and the other loopback addresses are reached over plain HTTP, so 443 is an ordinary port there and is kept. An empty value names no default registry. The value is judged when the configuration loads rather than by this schema, because the entry a name refers to may be declared in another configuration file: it is read after every configuration file and the `AGGREGA_DEFAULT_REGISTRY` environment variable, and refused in the same words whichever of them set it, naming that file or the variable. The `--registry` flag that names a publication's destination for one invocation is matched against the entries' names the same way; any other value it carries may be a reference, and the host that reference names is held to the same spelling and is where the publication lands, with no repository path. The gateway presents each connection's own credential as a bearer token, which Traefik Hub reads from the Secret the connection's Chat Completion middleware names, and a connection reaching a model whose `model.aggrega.ai/api` is not `openai`, or whose endpoint names an address rather than a host, halts the build. It publishes the route of the alias its `values.model` names as its `endpoint` and that alias as its `model`, and carries `model.aggrega.ai/api: openai`, so an agent's `model` socket takes it as it takes the AI gateway; with nothing wired it publishes both keys empty. A Release may name the gateway's callers in `infra.callers` and the htpasswd hashes of their keys through the `caller_keys` slot: Traefik Hub's API Key middleware then heads every model route and refuses a request presenting no declared key as `Authorization: Bearer <key>`, and the key is removed from the request forwarded; with no callers the routes are open. What Traefik Hub does with a caller's entry naming a Secret or a data key that does not exist is not stated in its reference, so in the worst case the routes are as open as with no callers. Of the controls below it realizes the period budget, the semantic cache for the callers it declares, prompt deny patterns and data masking, through middlewares of Traefik Hub's AI gateway, and the fallback chain and the retry policy, through Traefik's own failover and retry, each written into the routes its chart Recipe renders. The AI gateway is an entitlement carried inside the licence, which no build can see, and what Traefik Hub does with a valid token whose licence lacks it is undocumented, so attaching any of the first four halts the build until the Release sets `infra.ai_gateway_entitled` to `true`. Its realizations of prompt-injection screening, audit logging, target selection and response validation halt every attachment, each naming why, and the concurrency limit does not attach to it, since it carries no `dataplane.aggrega.ai/concurrency-cap` value. That a running gateway enforces any of these controls is not observed by any build.

b4106619100a06f7: **Choosing between targets:** `core/target-selection` declares how a gateway chooses among several targets that can serve the same request, with a `strategy` of `latency` (the target observed to answer quickest) or `cost` (the target cheapest to call). The strategy is part of what the application asks of its gateway, so the developer attaches it in the Aggregate. On the AI gateway the targets are the entries of its `values.models` that publish the same alias — a wired model is served under its connection's alias, which no other entry may publish — and the standard library realizes `latency` by writing the proxy's `latency-based-routing` into the routing configuration the gateway's Recipe renders: the proxy sends each request to the entry whose last ten replies took the least time on average, per output token where a reply reports its tokens, or to its first token for a streamed request, and an entry not yet tried counts as quickest. Without the attachment the configuration names no strategy, and the proxy picks among those entries at random. `cost` is refused by name there: the proxy prices an entry by looking its target up, exactly as written, in a price table that names OpenAI's and Anthropic's models without the provider prefix the gateway's targets carry, and prices an entry it does not find at a fixed fallback, so the entries sharing an alias would be priced alike and chosen by their order. On `core/gateway/kong-enterprise` every attachment halts, because each model wired to it is served on routes of its own carrying that one model, which leaves nothing to choose between. On `core/gateway/agentgateway` every attachment halts too, naming why: agentgateway draws two of a model name's targets at random and takes the one whose health, divided by the time it has taken to answer, scores higher, so the quickest target is taken only when it is drawn, and it chooses no target by cost. On `core/gateway/higress` every attachment halts too, naming why: Higress can measure a service's latency, but its load-balancer plugin runs after the AI proxy — which has already set the request's model, address and credential for the candidate the route resolved — and writes its choice into a request header nothing routes by without an Envoy filter this catalog does not render, so the choice does not take effect, and it chooses no target by cost. On `core/gateway/traefik-hub` every attachment halts too, naming why: Traefik picks by lowest response time only among the servers of one Service, which one model name and one credential cover, and between Services balances by weight or by a hash of the client's address, never by latency, and none of its strategies chooses a target by cost; and each model wired to the gateway is served on a route of its own carrying that one model, which leaves nothing to choose between. On any other gateway an attachment halts the build.

b45d256c60882e75: **Missing-key behaviour — tolerated on value templates; strict `missingkey=error` on path templates, on assertions, and on a `source:` coordinate.** Value templates evaluate with Go's `missingkey=zero` option, so a template referencing an unbound key (e.g., `.values.unset_field`) does not raise an error and the read renders nothing. Catalog idioms like `{{ .values.optional_field | default "fallback" }}` continue to work under this policy, because an unset value counts as empty for `default`. Path templates (`directory:` / `subDirectory:` on Release boundaries) evaluate with `missingkey=error` against a closed allowlist — silent path failures produce broken filesystem layouts that operators only discover post-build, and the strictness catches the error earlier. Two further surfaces take the same strict policy, for the same reason: an empty rendering there would produce a wrong verdict or a wrong pin rather than a field the author can read back. They are an `assertions:` entry on a Component, Feature, Recipe or FeatureRecipe, and the templated fields of a structured `source:` block on a Recipe or FeatureRecipe. [`errors/fatal-halts.md`](errors/fatal-halts.md) accounts for every surface's policy one by one and gives the presence-aware forms that work under the strict one.

b4846fa5efbc18c5: **A catalog entity named with a Release is checked as a single entity, in that Release's terms.** A `file` holding a Component, a Feature, a Recipe, a FeatureRecipe or a Plugin, sent with a `release`, gets the check [`aggrega validate <path> --release <release>`](aggrega-validate.md#checking-an-entity-in-a-releases-terms) runs, over the editor's unsaved buffer: its references — the Component a Recipe implements, a library a pillar refers to — resolve through the catalog directories the workspace configuration gives that Release, so one file can be clean in the terms of the Release that builds with it and fail in the terms of a Release whose directories do not hold what it refers to. That is the verdict the command line and the `validate` tool of [`aggrega mcp`](aggrega-mcp.md) give for the same entity beside the same Release, and like theirs it walks no closure and reads no lockfile. A blocking finding is one error entry in the check's own words and carrying its codes, drawn on the key it names in the entity and, where it names none, on the entity's `kind:` key, as [What a diagnostic entry carries](#what-a-diagnostic-entry-carries) describes — unless a build already reports that fault on the file, in which case the build's entry is the one report; an advisory the check raises while reading the catalog is a warning entry ahead of it; a clean check over directories that are all there answers no entry. A failed assertion — one that calls `fail`, in the Recipe or in the Component it implements — is not a blocking finding here but a warning entry, in the check's words and carrying its codes, closed by the sentence `A Release must satisfy this assertion before a build of it can pass.`, and drawn where the blocking finding would be: a Recipe's assertion on that assertion's own key under `assertions`, a Component's on the Recipe's `kind:` key. Like a blocking finding, it gives way to a build's entry reporting the same fault on the file. The check builds the entity around placeholders and schema defaults rather than the values a Release sets, so it cannot tell an assertion waiting on a Release from one that is broken, and leaves the verdict to a build, which reports the same assertion as an error ([a failed assertion is a warning](aggrega-validate.md#a-failed-assertion-is-a-warning)). A directory the workspace configuration lists for the Release where nothing exists is read as holding nothing, as every command reads it, so the check's verdict is the one it gives with that directory not listed — and a warning entry ahead of every other names the directory, in the line `aggrega pull` and `aggrega build` print for it ([Where local entities are read from](configuration.md#where-local-entities-are-read-from)). A `release` naming no file, or naming a directory, is answered on the file with the sentence the command line refuses it with, rather than checked in the workspace's terms. What a build of one cannot stand in for is judged as the command line judges it, and what the command line sets aside or does not check answers no entry here — see [what single-entity correctness does not check](aggrega-validate.md#what-single-entity-correctness-does-not-check), and, for a Recipe whose template reads a value only a topology edge or an attached credential delivers, [single-entity correctness](aggrega-validate.md#single-entity-correctness-an-entity-path). The Release's own Aggregate, a Manifest, a Release and a library are not checked one at a time, because the single-entity check does not take those kinds; they keep the closure's checks above. A buffer holding Workload content is read as YAML that is not an Aggrega document, because that content is written inside a Recipe's or a FeatureRecipe's `workload:` field and is checked there, where it sits; the command line and the `validate` tool, handed a Workload file by path, check its shape on its own.

b72082abcec3ac99: **What the core resolves.** No provider validates source keys of its own. A *fetched* source is resolved by a built-in identity whose `kind` selects a resolver — `helm-oci-chart`, `helm-https-chart`, `compose-https-fragment`, and `git-repository`. A fetch-intended source must carry `kind` and `url`; which further coordinate selects the content depends on the kind. The chart and fragment kinds take `version`, and pin it as written. `git-repository` takes `ref` — a tag, a branch, or a commit — and optionally `module_subdir`, naming the directory inside the repository that is the artifact; because only a commit names content that cannot be repointed, the reference is resolved at lock time and the lockfile records both the reference that was authored and the commit it resolved to. A `module_subdir` that climbs above the repository as written — a backslash counts as a separator — is refused before anything is fetched. The repository is archived from its own checkout: a symbolic link it commits is archived as the file or directory it points to where that lies inside the repository, and one leading out of it halts the pull, naming the link by its place in the repository. A structured source whose `url:` names a filesystem path is not fetched: it is read from disk on the same terms as a bare path string, with a relative `url:` anchored to the directory holding the entity file that declares it. A structured source that omits `kind`/`url` is not fetched either, and if a fetch was intended the build halts loudly at lock-time source descent rather than silently resolving to nothing. The content always pins ahead of time; the compiler never fetches live runtime state.

**Domain 2: The Split Schema (`usesSchema` & `schema`)**
To prevent the Platform Catalog from fragmenting into unmanageable schema files, Aggrega utilizes a Split Schema engine. The Native YAML `usesSchema` strictly defines and validates the topology, while `schema:` (JSON Schema 2020-12 — typically authored via the compact-form shorthand) validates the content of the `values` and `infra` pillars and declares the shape of the `provides` pillar. The `values` a developer authors and the `infra` an operator sets are checked against their declared types; the `provides` sub-schema declares the key names and types of the downstream contract a Recipe produces, and the compiler checks that every `inject` reference names a declared `provides` key — but the produced `provides` values themselves travel downstream as opaque strings the compiler pipes without interpretation, not values it type-checks, because the core does not interpret what a piped value means. **The `usesSchema` is where a socket is *declared*, and declaring one is what gives it a contract.** A socket the catalog entity declares carries that entity's constraints: a selector saying which targets it may reach, an `inject` allowlist, and per-edge `valueSchema` / `infraSchema`. Inside the `usesSchema`, Platform Architects use the `selector:` field — read as the string the Architect wrote, not copied into any generated schema — and the native Go selector engine evaluates it to enforce **Cross-Node Type Safety** over declared sockets. It ensures that if a socket requires a database, the developer cannot plug in a web server.

A guest decodes its input and encodes its output through the entry points its kit's `ImportInput` and `ImportOutput` already carry — `DecodeCBOR` and `EncodeCBOR` in Go, `decode_cbor` and `encode_cbor` in Rust, `decodeCBORImportInput` and `encodeCBORImportOutput` in TypeScript — reading and writing bytes (`Vec<u8>` in Rust, `Host.inputBytes()` and `Host.outputBytes(...)` in TypeScript). An importer that cannot complete says why in the output's `error`, and the import halts naming the importer and that message; an answer that is not an `ImportOutput` in this encoding — one written as JSON, or one carrying a top-level field the shape does not declare — halts the import too, naming the importer and its `import` export. bd11eafb0352095f: **Aggrega: Cache…** — choose a cache operation, then run it through the language server. Pressed on the Commands panel, the four are offered as a menu beside the button; run from here, they are offered as a list you pick from. Nothing is spawned, and each answer comes back as a structured result the panel reports: **status** lists every cache, what it holds and how far each one is shared, and removes nothing; **prune** removes the entries no lockfile references and names what it kept, together with anything it had no basis to reclaim and the operation that would; **evict** asks for a size cap first — a byte quantity such as `5GiB` or `512MiB`, or a byte count, read by the same parser the command line uses — and trims the shared compiled-module cache down to it; **clear** empties every cache. The three that remove something ask you to confirm first, and each confirmation names the caches that operation actually reaches: emptying reaches this workspace's own entity, source-artifact and external-input caches *and* the compiled-module, plugin-describe, docs-bundle and cli-plugin caches every project on this machine shares; pruning reaches the same workspace caches *and* the shared compiled-module, plugin-describe and cli-plugin caches; and trimming reaches only the shared compiled-module cache. Every size these operations report is written in the same vocabulary that cap is read in, so a figure you read off a cache report is one you can type straight into the cap prompt. A cap the compiler cannot read comes back with the compiler's own message naming what a size cap looks like. Cleared and trimmed caches repopulate on the next build that needs them. Windows refuses to remove a file another process has open, and a prune, a trim or an emptying then leaves it in place and goes on with the rest rather than failing: the Aggrega output channel names each entry a prune or a trim left, with its class, how far it is shared and its size, and gives, under each cache an emptying reached, how many files it left there and their size; the message the operation ends in says how many were left in place, asks you to run the operation again once that process has finished, and points you at the channel for which. **`mcp.authorization.issuer` and `mcp.authorization.resource` say who issues the tokens callers
present, and what this server is called as the resource they are issued for.** Both are required
whenever the `http` transport is chosen, and a listener is refused before anything binds without them, because
every request to the endpoint is answered with a bearer-token challenge and a challenge that names
nowhere to go is one a client cannot act on. Write whole addresses, scheme and host included: the
issuer exactly as that authorization server states its own identifier, and the resource as the
address your callers actually reach — the host a proxy in front presents, where there is one, rather
than the address this process binds. Both are published, with no credential asked for, in the OAuth
protected-resource metadata document the listener serves, which is where a client looks to find out
where to obtain a token. Neither holds anything secret: a token arrives on the request that
presents it and is never written in a configuration file. The issuer is an `https` address unless
the authorization server runs on this machine — `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `::1` — and a listener
naming a plain `http` issuer on any other host is refused before anything binds, whichever way it
reads its keys and its callers: every client is sent to the issuer to obtain its token, so over plain
`http` its authorization code and its token would cross the network unprotected, and where the keys
are read from there too, whoever sits on that path could substitute them.

**`mcp.authorization.jwks_file` names a file holding the keys tokens are verified against**, instead
of reading them from the authorization server. Leave it out and the server reads that server's
metadata at its well-known address and follows the `jwks_uri` published there, which is what a
workspace with network access does. That key address is held to the same rule as the issuer, and so
is any address either read is redirected to: one that is plain `http` on another host is never
asked, and a token needing those keys is answered `503` until the authorization server publishes its
metadata and keys over `https`. Set it and the authorization server is never contacted — which
is what a workspace declaring `offline: true` needs, and such a workspace is refused before its
listener binds unless this names a file. It is a path and follows the rule above: a relative one
resolves against the directory of the file that declared it, so a key set committed beside that file
is found wherever the server is launched from. The file holds public verification keys, which are
what an authorization server publishes — nothing that signs, and nothing secret.

The accessors listed below are stable across patch releases; renames or removals are signalled by a release-notes entry and a deprecation cycle, and adding a new accessor within a package is additive and does not break existing matchers. A code is fixed once its condition is published, so it is the identifier to record wherever a condition has to be named durably: renaming an accessor does not move the code its condition was registered under, and a code you have recorded outlives a refactor of the Go surface. A short code is the most durable of the three: a number is handed out once and then fixed, and a retired condition's number stays retired rather than being handed to a different condition, so a short code recorded in an old report still names the condition it named when it was recorded. That is enforced rather than merely intended — a condition declared under a retired number is refused before the compiler reads any input, on every run — and every retired number is published beside the live ones in [the table of every condition](#every-condition-by-short-code). The code column below carries the code, and it is the value a client of the structured diagnostic reads without linking these packages. It is published rather than inferred, because it need not restate the row it sits on — a re-exported name reports the code of the condition it forwards to, and a rule's code names the rule rather than the accessor. The message column is the literal text the sentinel renders; the user-facing diagnostic puts a bracketed head and the source location ahead of that text. That head carries the condition's short code, with the occurrence's category beside it where the occurrence has one, as in `[DEVELOPER_ERROR E0007]` — so a reader can resolve either independently: the categories (`DEVELOPER_ERROR` / `OPS_ERROR` / `CATALOG_ERROR` / `TRANSLATION_ERROR` / `FETCH_ERROR` / `POLICY_ERROR` / `TRUST_ERROR`) are taught in [error-translation.md](./error-translation.md), and the short codes resolve in [the table of every condition](#every-condition-by-short-code) on this page.
