c357df0d60816971: **Flat Compilation & Feature Atomicity:** Aggrega does not manage state, ping endpoints, or wait for a rollout to finish. The compiler evaluates nested modules and resolves them down into a flat, 1-dimensional Intermediate Representation (IR) graph before passing the data to the Wasm rendering plugins. Crucially, while the graph is flattened, the compiler preserves **Feature Atomicity**. If a proxy feature autonomously declares a network edge to a secure vault, the compiler records the semantic origin of that edge, ensuring Wasm policy engines can execute $O(1)$ lookups without falsely attributing the connection to the parent component. Finally, to support temporal sequencing, each boundary in the Release carries a `syncWave: <integer>` value; each rendering plugin translates the per-boundary wave into whatever its own target expresses ordering with — an execution-order annotation the downstream GitOps controller reads, or a dependency between the services of the file it renders — while a target with no ordering surface at all records the wave without sequencing on it.

The FeatureRecipe's `valuesMapping` writes that config as a **mounted compose config** — a top-level `configs:` entry with inline `content:`, referenced from the gateway and mounted at `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf`; it is not an operator-mounted concern — and names every bridged endpoint under the gateway's `x-aggrega-networks-of`, which this provider resolves into the networks those endpoints are placed on ([below](#joining-the-networks-of-other-components--x-aggrega-networks-of)). This is the per-leaf unit of the sensitivity marking, and it answers a question neither of the other two does — sensitive gives one answer for the whole attachment, sensitive_inject gives one per inject delivery key, and neither names an individual leaf. A leaf appears where a path the Feature's schema declares sensitive covers it: the declaration names that leaf, or names an object containing it, so a leaf beneath an object a declaration covers is named by that declaration. Matching runs segment-wise over the dotted path, with nothing read out of the path's own text and no value inspected, so a declaration at `db` covers `db.password` and does not reach a sibling leaf named `dbPassword`. The per-attachment answer is never spread across individual leaves, which would assert something false about a leaf left readable. An absent key states that this attachment names no leaf its Feature declares sensitive. It does not assert that the payload is insensitive, and it does not separate an attachment that has no such leaf to name from a producer that does not report this axis at all — a guest that reads an absent key as permission to display or emit a value in the clear has read it backwards. The marking is part of this payload's contract rather than a response to any one plugin: a policy that needs it can be written whenever the need arises, without the payload having to be widened first to make it expressible, so a plugin finding this key absent learns what absence states above and nothing about whether anything reads the key. Leaves arrive in the order the payload holds them, the values pillar's before the infra pillar's — the same order the values and infra payloads themselves carry, and what makes the payload byte-identical across runs of identical input. c9c02f14b90c1cea: **Caller-Identity Propagation, at two hops:** The original caller's identity has to survive two different hops, and each is protected at a different place. At the **gateway hop**, the developer attaches `core/context-propagation` to the gateway a request enters through, which selects on `dataplane.aggrega.ai/caller-identity`. At **compile-time**, the attachment is realized in that gateway's own configuration — on Envoy Gateway, a client traffic policy that verifies each client's certificate against an authority the Release names and forwards the certificate's details; on the LiteLLM AI gateway, a request hook that removes any identity header a caller supplied and adds the user and team of the virtual key the gateway verified, and its organization where the key names one, on requests to the model aliases the attachment lists in `destinations`. At **runtime**, the service behind the gateway receives who called rather than only that the gateway called. At the **workload hop**, a request one agent makes directly to another never crosses that gateway, so it is checked at the receiving agent's own ingress, where a service mesh rejects any request lacking a signed token proving the original user's intent (e.g., an Istio JWT `AuthorizationPolicy`). The standard library ships the gateway-hop Feature and no workload-hop Feature, so attaching `core/context-propagation` protects the traffic that passes through a gateway and leaves agent-to-agent calls to mesh configuration the enterprise supplies itself. An agent another party runs, which `core/ai-tool/agent-invocation` reaches over A2A as `core/ai-agent/a2a-remote`, sits outside the Release altogether: that party checks each call against the security scheme the agent's Agent Card declares, and the tool presents the credential held on its connection, read from a Secret by reference, under the request header the agent publishes. Where the card requires OAuth 2.0 client credentials or OpenID Connect, the connection holds a client secret instead, or as well, with the client id the operator writes on it, and the agent publishes the token or discovery address and the scopes its card declares; the tool's own container obtains the token with them, refreshes it and presents it on each call; the catalog delivers only those inputs, and no build can check what the container does with them. Where the card requires mutual TLS, the connection holds a client certificate, and, where an authority the image does not already trust signs the agent's server certificate, that authority too; each is mounted into the tool's container as files from a Secret the connection names, and the container presents the certificate in the TLS handshake itself. So the tool reaches an agent whose card declares an API key in a header or a cookie, an HTTP authentication scheme whose value is fixed, such as Bearer or Basic, with the Secret holding the whole header value, OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect with the client-credentials grant, or mutual TLS. It does not reach one whose card requires a key in the query string, an HTTP scheme answering a challenge from the agent, such as Digest, or an OAuth 2.0 flow other than client credentials. Nor does it present a credential to an agent another party runs over plain HTTP: where that agent's address is `http`, a credential or a client secret on the connection halts the build, naming the connection, because the credential, or the token obtained with the secret, would travel to it unencrypted. An agent running inside the Release stays reachable over `http` with either, and the credential then crosses the cluster network unencrypted.

ca47b6e925aafdf5: **What the core resolves today.** Per-provider Wasm source validation is not yet implemented. A *fetched* source is resolved by a built-in identity whose `kind` selects a resolver — today `helm-oci-chart`, `helm-https-chart`, `compose-https-fragment`, and `git-repository`. A fetch-intended source must carry `kind` and `url`; which further coordinate selects the content depends on the kind. The chart and fragment kinds take `version`, and pin it as written. `git-repository` takes `ref` — a tag, a branch, or a commit — and optionally `module_subdir`, naming the directory inside the repository that is the artifact; because only a commit names content that cannot be repointed, the reference is resolved at lock time and the lockfile records both the reference that was authored and the commit it resolved to. A `module_subdir` that climbs above the repository as written — a backslash counts as a separator — is refused before anything is fetched. The repository is archived from its own checkout: a symbolic link it commits is archived as the file or directory it points to where that lies inside the repository, and one leading out of it halts the pull, naming the link by its place in the repository. A structured source whose `url:` names a filesystem path is not fetched: it is read from disk on the same terms as a bare path string, with a relative `url:` anchored to the directory holding the entity file that declares it. A structured source that omits `kind`/`url` is not fetched either, and if a fetch was intended the build halts loudly at lock-time source descent rather than silently resolving to nothing. When the per-provider Wasm socket ships, it validates provider-specific shapes and translates them ahead-of-time into a deterministic fetch identity — the content always pins ahead-of-time; the compiler never fetches live runtime state.

**The Dual-State Injection Context (Null-Safety vs. Intent Purity)**
When generating configurations for Modifiers (the FeatureRecipe bound to any attachment, credential or otherwise), the compiler must balance null-pointer safety for Go templates, dynamic network routing, and the preservation of a capability-agnostic graph. To achieve this, the compiler provides a dual-state context to the template:

cac3a7fec22c7151: **`scope`** — the document root the export operates on: `own` (the node's own rendered documents) or `host` (the documents of the component a component-scope FeatureRecipe is attached to). Before a pipeline step's plugin runs, the host reads the step's declared export scope and enforces that the provider rendering that scope's documents appears in the plugin's `spec.pipelineStep.capabilities` (Section 5) — an `own`-scope export is checked against the provider rendering the node's own documents, a `host`-scope export against the host component's provider, and an empty scope defaults to `own` for this check. cd0301a127a9ce04: Machine-generated record of the plugin identity trusted for each attachment that returns an accept-or-reject verdict — a `plugins.governance` attachment in an `ir-verdict` or `render-verdict` role, and every `plugins.linter` attachment. Lives at `plugins-trust.yaml` beside the lockfile and is committed alongside it, because a record held outside version control is one nobody can review and nothing can compare against. Written by `aggrega pull`, which creates the file the first time it resolves one of those attachments and adds a record per attachment as it resolves it. A file carrying records for only some of the configured attachments is a valid intermediate state rather than a damaged one. Read by `aggrega build`, by `aggrega lint --release` and by `aggrega validate --release`, and by the same operations reached through `aggrega serve` and `aggrega mcp`; each holds the workspace configuration to the record before any of those attachments runs. Two disagreements are refused, for different reasons: a plugin whose resolved artifact digest is not the digest recorded for it is refused rather than run, because the plugin that would run is not the one the record was reviewed for; and a record entry that no configured verdict attachment accounts for halts the run, because dropping a gate changes no rendered byte, so output produced without a gate that was reviewed is indistinguishable from output that gate approved. A build, a release-scoped lint and a release-scoped validation — from the command line, through `aggrega serve` or through `aggrega mcp` — also hold each of those plugins they read from the content cache to the `signature` its record carries, when they load it, as a build holds every lockfile entry to the one that entry carries: see `signature` below. The opposite direction — a configured attachment the record does not yet hold — is the intermediate state just described and neither comparison refuses it, and an absent record holds no entries at all, so it pins nothing and neither comparison refuses anything over it; the signature requirement is the one hold a missing entry does not escape, as `signature` below describes. An entry leaves the record only on an explicit upgrade: `aggrega pull --upgrade` naming a plugin drops that plugin's entry when no verdict attachment names it any more, and a bare `aggrega pull --upgrade` drops every such entry. A plain `aggrega pull` neither re-resolves an entry's identity nor removes the entry, so a halt over an entry nothing accounts for is cleared by saying so deliberately rather than by the next run. A record whose last entry is dropped is emptied rather than deleted, and an emptied record is a valid one: it holds nothing, so it pins nothing and neither comparison refuses anything over it, exactly as an absent record does. Each record is addressed by the plugin's own identity coordinate and carries the selected version and the artifact digest as fields, so a version change is a change to a field of an existing record rather than a new record under a new address — which is what makes a re-versioned plugin distinguishable, in the file and in its diff, from one recorded for the first time. Besides that identity, a record carries two facts about the artifact it names, each recorded only when it was verified: the deprecation a publisher has attached to it, when one was found and its signature verified, and the verified-signature fact `aggrega pull` recorded when it verified the plugin's own signature — the same fact, under the same key, a lockfile entry carries. Each is a fact about the recorded artifact rather than a second identity, which is why an ordinary pull records one without disturbing the identity it is held to. What the file records beyond those is nothing: no signature over the file itself, no rule inputs, no resolution provenance — no registry host, no path on the machine that wrote it — and no clock reading, so the same resolution produces the same bytes wherever and whenever it runs. A `plugins.governance` verdict attachment's external rule files are recorded as digests in the lockfile's `verdict_inputs`; a `plugins.linter` attachment's rule inputs are recorded in neither file. Everything a build reproduces byte-for-byte is pinned in the lockfile instead; a verdict attachment shapes none of the rendered output, which is why its identity is recorded here rather than there. Schema evolution discipline: adding a new top-level section is SemVer-MINOR (additive); adding a new field inside an existing section is SemVer-MINOR; removing a key or tightening a constraint is SemVer-MAJOR.

cd922dea228f5c52: Map of file name to file-content authoring, shaped exactly as this Recipe's own `artifacts`: the same three modes — an inline Go template string, a `$import:` of a local Go-template file, or a `$import:` of an ArtifactLibrary bundle, whose files nest under the entry's key as `<key>/<filename>` — the same key-to-filename rule, and the same template context, so an entry may read `.values`, `.infra`, `.locals` and the rest exactly as an `artifacts` entry does. What differs is where each file is written: once, in the directory holding the boundary's assembled output, beside the files the provider's own assembly writes there, rather than in this component's own directory. Every entry is evaluated for each component this Recipe renders in the boundary, and the files those evaluations produce are merged by name: one name evaluated to identical bytes by several components, or by several Recipes, is one file, while one name evaluated to different bytes halts the build naming the file and every contributor, as does a name the provider's own assembly already writes. Nothing is stamped into such a file to say which component wrote it, because it belongs to every component that declared it. An entry whose template renders to nothing writes no file. The entries are not handed to the provider, which writes the rest of the boundary's output without reading them. In the object form, `$import` must not match `^oci://`; a value that does is rejected. Keys: The key names the file, so it is bounded to a single filename, under the rule an `artifacts` key follows: it begins with a letter or digit and continues with letters, digits, dots, hyphens or underscores. A `/` would make one key name a path rather than a file, and a leading `.` would admit `..`, which names a location outside the boundary's output directory — the first character class refuses both. For a library import the key names the directory the bundle's files are nested under, so the same bound applies. Pattern: `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*$`.

cdcf84923c030f87:
**Directories listed under `workspace.catalog_dirs` are read as well, and they are read first.**
The list is an ordered search stack: the first directory to declare an identity owns it, and the
same identity in a later directory is shadowed. `catalog` is read after everything listed — unless
a listed directory already contains it, in which case it is read as part of that directory — so
listing a directory adds to what you had rather than replacing it. A repeatable `--catalog <dir>`
on the command line is read ahead of both, and a relative path given there resolves against the
directory you ran the command from, since no configuration file declared it. A directory named more
than once — on the command line and in the list, or twice in the list — is read once, at the place it
was first named, so nothing in it is reported as shadowed by itself: a shadow is always two different
files declaring one identity. Two spellings of one directory, a path to it through a link, and — on a
file system that ignores case — a spelling in another case all name that one directory. A directory
inside another listed directory is still read as its own entry. A project that keeps a
catalog variant per Release can give each Release a list of its own instead — see
[Giving a Release its own catalog directories](#giving-a-release-its-own-catalog-directories).

cde78a6f86e77be9: **Send `target` to draft the Manifest the drafted Release builds against for one provider.** `target` is a provider capability — the word a Recipe's `spec.capability` binds to, such as `compose` or `helm` — and it is `aggrega import`'s `--target`, composed by the same operation, so a call and the command draft the same files from the same source. For each component type and each feature type the drafts need — on the drafted Aggregate's components, their connections and its subsystems, on the catalog Aggregates it composes, and on the drafted Release's attachments — in the order the drafts first declare it, the import looks in the workspace's catalog for the Recipes, or for a feature type the feature recipes, that implement the type and bind to that capability. Where there is exactly one — several versions of one count as one — the Manifest maps the type to it by its capability-qualified name with no version, such as `compose/postgres`, which the first pull pins in the lockfile at the highest version available. Where there are several of different names, it maps the one named after the type itself, such as `helm/postgres` for `core/datastore/postgres`. Where there is none, or several with none so named, the type is left unmapped and a `warn` entry in `diagnostics` names it and why — the several each by name — so a build of the drafts stops naming each instance or attachment of it, under [No Recipe is mapped for a component or feature instance](../errors/fatal-halts.md#no-recipe-is-mapped-for-a-component-or-feature-instance), until the mapping is added. Where the importer drafts the Manifest itself, to choose the Recipe one instance renders through or a feature recipe among several, each mapping it wrote that the catalog offers for that type and capability is kept, any other is dropped with a `warn` entry, and the types it leaves are mapped as above. The Manifest is drafted as `manifest.yaml` beside the drafted Release, named and versioned as the Release is, and the Release's `spec.manifest` is set to that name — the comment the importer wrote in its place is replaced, and nothing else in the Release changes. A Release that already names a Manifest is left as it is, and where the import drafts no Release the Manifest is drafted beside the Aggregate, with its name and version, and an `info` entry says nothing references it. The Manifest and the edited Release are drafts like the others: in `written`, in the record, and handed back under `dry_run`. A `target` no Recipe in the catalog binds to is refused before the importer runs, under [An import's target names a capability no Recipe in the catalog binds to](../errors/fatal-halts.md#an-imports-target-names-a-capability-no-recipe-in-the-catalog-binds-to), naming it as you sent it and the capabilities the catalog's Recipes bind to, and nothing is written. ce045d32068e3ae4: **A retired number is listed too, in its own set of notes beneath the table, and it stays listed permanently.** A condition is occasionally withdrawn — it is replaced by one covering more ground, or nothing ever reported it — and from that moment its number is retired: it is never handed to a different condition, so a short code you quote off an old report can only ever name what it named when the report was written. That promise is mechanical rather than editorial. A condition declared under a retired number is refused before the compiler reads any input, on every run, so no release can carry one — the same class of refusal a number two live conditions tried to share would meet, worded so you can tell which of the two you hit. ce3ec3c000ac686b: JSON Schema 2020-12 content covering the free-form pillars: values (the Developer's domain — application-shape parameters the Developer configures per Feature attachment in the Aggregate); infra (the Operator's domain — physical sizing knobs supplied by the Release); and provides (downstream context keys this Feature exposes to consumers via the topology pipe). Accepts three authoring modes via content-shape dispatch: (1) inline content (a YAML map carrying compact form, JSON Schema YAML, or mixed); (2) file replacement via {$import: <path>}, written at spec.schema to supply the whole contract from one file or at a single pillar to supply that pillar alone, with a relative path read against the directory holding the entity that declared it; (3) cross-document reference via {$ref: <Library>#/schemas/<name>} into a SchemaLibrary entry by bare-name identity (the version is supplied by the per-Release lockfile; no registry host appears in the reference). ce41d569b0d26c6f: A Feature may declare `spec.extends: <feature-name>` pointing to a base Feature whose authoring surface it inherits. The reference names the base by its `metadata.name`, not by the registry coordinate the Feature publishes under, and takes the same three version forms every catalog reference takes: bare (`core/queue`) for the highest available release, exact (`core/queue:1.0.0`), or a caret range (`core/queue:^1.0.0`). The compiler walks the parent chain at catalog load, validates that the chain is acyclic, then merges parent specs into the child to produce a single resolved Feature. The child's authored fields take precedence on key collision; the parent's `metadata.labels` and `metadata.annotations`, `appliesTo` / `appliesToAnyOf` selectors, `interoperability` block, `usesSchema`, `featuresSchema`, and the JSON Schema 2020-12 declarations on `schema` are auto-merged downward. Every other `metadata` field is the child's verbatim, so identity and provenance never inherit.

A guest reads and writes it through the entry points its kit's payload type already carries — `DecodeCBOR` and `EncodeCBOR` in Go, `decode_cbor` and `encode_cbor` in Rust, `decodeCBORMutatorInput` and `encodeCBORMutatorOutput` in TypeScript — so no CBOR library is needed and nothing hand-parses bytes. The graph's `nodes`, each node's `labels`, and each node's `values` are maps the schema marks order-preserving, so they cross as [ordered lists of entries](#maps-that-keep-their-order) — the nodes in the order the build holds them, which is author order, each node's labels in the order the node carries them, and each node's values in the order the Aggregate writes them — and a guest reads all three through its kit's order-keeping container. d0fdd2695c357980: A registry host has one reading. Each `registries[].host` is written as the host itself — a lowercase host name containing a dot, `localhost`, a single name followed by a port, an IPv4 address, or an IPv6 address in brackets, each with an optional `:port`, and no scheme, path, credentials or capital letters — because that spelling is the key every per-registry trust policy is found under, and the official hub's built-in signature requirement is keyed on `hub.aggrega.ai`. `default_registry` names a host the same way, and may follow it with a repository path, such as `ghcr.io/acme`: everything published through the default then lands under that path, and every short reference resolves under it, while trust is still decided by the host alone. `default_registry` may instead be written as the `name:` of a `registries` entry, and then stands for that entry's host. The name is read once, as the configuration resolves, against the entries in force after every configuration file and the environment, so every reader of the default — publishing, the location binding, signature verification and every trust lookup — reads that one entry's host, and none of them reaches a host spelled like the name; a name followed by a path is refused, since a name stands for an entry rather than a location. A name is matched before a host spelling, and a name two entries carry is refused as ambiguous. The same reading decides three things a pull does with the host: the registry location a host-less catalog identity is bound to, whether the fetched artifact names a registry whose signature is checked at all, and which trust policy that check runs against. A spelling that could reach a registry while missing its policy — capitals, an explicit default HTTPS port, a scheme, credentials, a path on a `registries` entry's host — is refused where it is configured, naming the spelling to write, and so is a single name with no port that names no entry, which is the shape of a catalog identity's first segment rather than of a host. The refusal applies on every layer that can set the value: the configuration file, where the schema states the same shape as a pattern on each `registries[].host`; the `AGGREGA_DEFAULT_REGISTRY` environment variable; and the command line. So every host a configuration can name is one whose artifacts are verified under the policy written for it. The host is judged by its spelling alone; whether the name resolves, or a registry answers there, is runtime state the compiler never fetches. [configuration](../language-reference/cli/configuration.md#how-a-registry-host-is-written) spells out the accepted forms with examples.

**The requests that go out to a registry divide into the ones that read and the ones that publish.**
`aggrega/resolveDependencies` fetches what a Release needs, and
`aggrega/build` joins it when — and only when — its `autoPull` field asks it to resolve
dependencies first, in which case it reaches a registry and writes the lockfile before it renders;
`aggrega/registryUpdate` walks every configured registry to rebuild the local search index;
`aggrega/pluginAdd` searches the configured registry for the plugin a request names and reads its
published versions to pin one; `aggrega/registryAdd` asks the registry it registers for the trust
policy that registry advertises, unless the request declines the fetch or supplies a policy of its
own, and `aggrega/configInit` asks the registry it is seeding for the same; `aggrega/explainError` acquires the documentation bundle it reads
a condition's walk-through from, once, where the cache every project on the machine shares holds no copy the
workspace's own signature check admits — see [`aggrega explain`](aggrega-explain.md);
`aggrega/import` fetches a core importer from the workspace's default registry, once, where the
machine does not hold it yet — see [What an import response tells you](#what-an-import-response-tells-you); and
`aggrega/entityDefinition` reads the entity a registry reference names when one is sent as its `name`,
writing nothing.
`aggrega/publishEntity`, `aggrega/publishArtifact`, `aggrega/signArtifacts` and
`aggrega/deprecateArtifact` write to one — bytes, a signature, or a withdrawal marker. A request
reaches a registry only when it was sent to do that: a listing reports what the configuration pins, a
search reads an offline snapshot, and a publication asked for with `dryRun` computes what it would
send and contacts nobody.

d494cdd818e81423: **Why explicit `exportedComponents:` rather than default-export.** The explicit contract is the discipline target: a child Aggregate's authors decide which internal nodes are part of the public interface and which remain implementation detail. Default-export-everything (where the parent reaches every internal component by name) would couple the parent to the child's internal layout, so refactoring the child's internals — renaming a node, splitting one component into two, swapping a worker for a managed service — would silently break parent code that named the now-absent node. The explicit listing carries an authoring cost (one declaration per exported node) and a maintenance benefit (internal refactors are non-breaking by default unless they touch the published interface). There is no shorthand or "expose all" convention; the explicit declaration is the architectural commitment.

It names the node's OWN data — what values_mapping and infra_mapping carry for this node — and is a different subject from the marking on an attachment entry, which names data an attachment carries against its Feature's declaration. Neither is recoverable from the other: a node's Component and an attachment's Feature declare different schemas, and a node that attaches nothing still carries values. The payload read here is the one those two mappings carry, so a leaf standing at a value the Component's schema declares as a default is named alongside one an author wrote — a filled default is a datum the graph carries, and a marking read off the written blocks alone would leave it unnamed. A leaf appears where a path the Component's schema declares sensitive covers it: the declaration names that leaf, or names an object containing it, so a leaf beneath an object a declaration covers is named by that declaration. Matching runs segment-wise over the dotted path, with nothing read out of the path's own text and no value inspected, so a declaration at `db` covers `db.password` and does not reach a sibling leaf named `dbPassword`. An absent key states that this node names no leaf its Component declares sensitive, which includes the case where the node's Component resolves to no schema this reader could read. It does not assert that the node's payload is insensitive, and it does not separate a node that has no such leaf to name from a producer that does not report this axis at all. A consumer that reads an absent key as permission to display or emit a value in the clear has read it backwards. Leaves arrive in the order the payload holds them, the values pillar's before the infra pillar's, which is the same order those payloads themselves carry and what keeps the graph byte-identical across runs of identical input. Each entry binds one provider capability (the bare capability name a Recipe binds through `spec.capability`, e.g. `helm` or `compose`) to the bare identity of the provider-rendering plugin that serves it (a Plugin entity's `metadata.name`, the `<socket>/<name>` path, e.g. `provider/helm`), with an optional trailing `:version` in the same three forms as a version pin (bare, exact `:1.0.0`, or major-compatible range `:^1.0.0`). This is the disambiguation and override surface for a federated catalog where more than one provider plugin serves the same capability: the binding selects which publisher's plugin renders that capability. When a capability is served by exactly one provider plugin no entry is needed. Exactly one entry per capability is permitted across the composed list; a duplicate capability halts resolution loudly. Resolution is at pull: the pull records the resolved binding into the per-Release lockfile, and the build reads the lockfile — a change here after a pull is not adopted until the next pull, so build output is invariant to it (deterministic output). Every build and every validation of a Release also checks each entry here, whether or not a Recipe asks for its capability: an entry naming a plugin the build holds that does not serve the entry's capability halts, naming what that plugin serves and a spelling one edit away when there is one; an entry naming a capability and no plugin, where no provider plugin the build reads serves that capability, is reported as a warning rather than halting, because the plugin serving it may be one only another Release reads; and an entry for a capability a plugin serves but this Release never asks for is legal and reported as nothing, since entries are written for the whole workspace and a build is of one Release. A `capability` containing a colon is refused when the configuration loads: a Recipe's `spec.capability` is read as the capability up to its last colon and a version pin after it, so no Recipe could reach such an entry. A missing entry for an unambiguously-served capability is not an error; a missing entry for an ambiguously-served capability halts the pull loudly, listing the candidate plugins. Version coexistence is preserved: the binding selects the plugin repository per capability, and each Recipe's own `spec.capability` version pin selects the version within that repository, so two Recipes pinning different versions of one provider still coexist. Default: `[]`
d9d54199df5e3bef: **What is pinned.** [`aggrega pin`](../cli/aggrega-pin.md) and the pull fetch the package and record two digests in the lockfile: the manifest digest, and the digest of the package layer exactly as it was published. The version is recorded as you wrote it. Every later build reads the package from the cache and verifies it against those digests before vendoring anything, so it needs no network. A tag is a name a registry can move to other content: a pull over a Recipe whose `entity.lock` records the earlier digest halts, naming `aggrega pin`, rather than adopting the new bytes, and running `aggrega pin` on the Recipe records the new ones deliberately. A `sha256:` version names content that cannot move.

da41ee218802624c: A plugin runs behind an ahead-of-time-purity firewall. The host loads and executes the module through an embedded Wasm runtime under a capability-denied configuration: no network sockets, no filesystem, no environment, discarded stdio, and an observable wall clock frozen to a build-invariant instant. Any I/O call a guest attempts fails at the call boundary, so a plugin cannot reach for runtime state. Author plugins with this firewall in mind: a plugin transforms the payload it is handed and returns a result the host consumes verbatim, and determinism is your responsibility — identical input must produce identical output bytes. The one sanctioned channel for remote content is the host-mediated external-input fetch (Section 4), which serves bytes under a digest-pinned discipline rather than giving the guest live network access.

**A budget per caller**, `scope: caller`. The gateway tells callers apart

da69fcc6d31ea385: **Wire encoding.** A step's input (`FRPStepInput`) and its answer (`FRPStepOutput`) travel as **canonical CBOR** ([RFC 8949](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8949) §4.2.1), in both directions. A guest decodes its input and encodes its answer through the entry points the payload types carry — `DecodeCBOR` and `EncodeCBOR` in Go, `decode_cbor` and `encode_cbor` in Rust (on the types the `aggrega-abi` crate publishes), `decodeCBORFRPStepInput` and `encodeCBORFRPStepOutput` in TypeScript — reading and writing bytes (`Vec<u8>` in Rust, `Host.inputBytes()` and `Host.outputBytes(...)` in TypeScript). No CBOR library is needed and nothing hand-parses bytes. The step's `with` input (`step_input`), the `outputs` it returns, and the `own` and `host` document sets are maps the schema marks order-preserving, so they cross as [ordered lists of entries](#maps-that-keep-their-order) in the order the pipeline holds them, and a guest reads and writes them through its kit's order-keeping container — which is what lets a step's outputs reach `.steps.<id>.outputs` in the order the step returned them. Each unit's `tree`, each value of `step_input` and `outputs`, a patch's `value`, a side effect's `crd` and the render `context` cross as the bytes of their JSON documents, which a guest parses as JSON to look inside; a unit's `bytes` cross as a raw byte run the generated decoder fills into the kit's own field type — a byte slice in Go, a base64 string in Rust and TypeScript. Each diagnostic crosses in the shared `Diagnostic` shape. An answer that is not an `FRPStepOutput` in this encoding — one written as JSON, or one carrying a top-level field the shape does not declare — fails the step, naming the function it runs, which halts the build unless the step is `optional`. Called directly with `aggrega plugin run-local --export step`, a step is handed the authored JSON payload converted into this encoding, and its answer is read as the export's output shape and printed as JSON — an answer that is not that shape is refused, naming the export, as a build refuses it.

The cap and its scope are capacity sizing the operator decides, set in the attachment's `infra`, so the operator attaches it in the Release. The cap is counted per running proxy, so where several replicas run each of them admits that many. It attaches to any component declaring `dataplane.aggrega.ai/concurrency-cap`, and a realization refuses by name the scope its gateway does not count. On `core/gateway/nginx` scope `gateway` is realized as NGINX's `limit_conn`, keyed on one word the same for every request, so NGINX counts every request it is processing as one total, kept in memory its worker processes share, and answers a request past the cap with HTTP 503; scope `model` is refused, since NGINX keeps no count for each upstream target, and so is a `max_in_flight` above 65535, the most `limit_conn` takes. On `core/gateway/envoy-gateway` scope `model` is realized as the circuit breaker of the traffic policy on the route serving the wired models, the policy that also carries a period budget's rate limit and the retry policy's retry: Envoy Gateway applies it to the backend of each rule of that route, and each wired model has a rule of its own, so at most `max_in_flight` requests are sent to each wired model at once, and a request past the cap is answered with HTTP 503 and is not sent again; a send the retry policy repeats counts against the cap like the first. Envoy's worker threads check the count and then add to it, so requests arriving together can take it briefly above the cap. Scope `gateway` is refused, since Envoy Gateway keeps a cap for each backend and none on their total, and so is an attachment with nothing wired to the `models` socket. On the AI gateway scope `model` is realized as the `max_parallel_requests` of every entry of its model map, typed by hand and wired alike: at most `max_in_flight` requests are in flight to each entry at once, and a request finding its entry full is answered with HTTP 429 — after the gateway's retries where its alias has one entry, and at once where it has several, even while another of them has room, since the proxy picks the entry before it counts — unless `core/fallback-chain` lists fallbacks for its alias, to which it is then sent on. The proxy keeps each count in memory, where by default a record lapses ten minutes after it is made and a new count then starts at zero, so the attachment also sets that lifetime to a century, keeping every count as long as the proxy runs. Because of that lifetime the gateway refuses a request carrying `priority` while the cap is attached, even where the Release admits the field, since the proxy keeps a queue entry for every such request until its record lapses; and the build halts on a model map of more than 100 entries, past which the store the counts are kept in, which holds 200 records and drops one whenever it is full, could drop a count. Scope `gateway` is refused there, since the proxy's one total is read only by a request limiter an environment variable switches on, which counts a request for its first second. Nor does the hosted gateway realize it: the request limit its terraform Recipe writes into the gateway's resource is a rate, a number of requests over an interval, rather than a cap on the requests in flight.

Each entry is itself a Go template, evaluated against a self-contained context: '.context.instance_id' (the HOST COMPONENT this attachment is resolving for, which is what that reference denotes on every template surface), '.attachment_name' (the attachment instance being resolved, and the only route to that name from a local), the attachment's own '.values' and '.infra', and the entries of this same block resolved so far. Both checks read the path a reference RESOLVES to rather than the keystrokes, so they cover the direct form, a read inside a '{{ with .locals }}' block, and a read through a variable bound directly to '.locals' alike. Two spellings they do not cover. One is a reference whose path the template text does not decide — one reached through a function, such as 'index .locals', or through a 'with' block or a variable binding whose pipeline applies one, since what such a pipeline yields is decided at evaluation rather than by its text. The other is a key read off a parenthesised block, '(.locals).<key>' or '($.locals).<key>', where the key hangs off the value the parentheses yield rather than off the block itself. Neither is analysed, and an absent key reached either way does not halt: it renders the literal text '<no value>' rather than nothing at all. The one exception is 'index' itself: on every template surface it halts, naming the key, when the map it reads does not hold the key it is asked for, so an absent key reached through 'index .locals' halts. This FeatureRecipe's locals resolve BEFORE its provides, so a provides template may read '.locals' and receives resolved values, while a provides template naming a key this block does not declare halts. The rules are the same ones a Recipe's locals block follows. Where executionScope is boundary, the block is evaluated once for the boundary attachment, against the boundary-scope template context rather than a component's, and every component the attachment reaches reads those resolved entries, the '.locals' its injectMapping reads included. dc92168c52437896: **Compiler Use Case:** It records who operates the component's underlying resource, letting a policy an operator attaches judge Data Exfiltration risk; the compiler reads the value as a string and judges nothing. When an Agent whose class label says it holds `internal` data connects to a Model labeled `managed` — a service operated outside the Release's own boundary — such a policy can read that the data leaves that boundary, and halt the build unless the connection is routed through an AI gateway carrying `core/data-masking`, which masks the chat and completion text the gateway forwards. An agent's `model` socket takes such a gateway in place of the model, so that route is an edge of the graph the policy reads, and a model the gateway serves from its `models` socket is an edge of its own, from the gateway to the model component, whose labels the policy reads — so the path from an agent through the gateway to a `managed` model is in the graph end to end. An upstream typed by hand into the gateway's model map is not: it is a string the compiler does not resolve, so a policy reading the graph sees the gateway and nothing behind it. [examples/policy-data-class-route](../language-reference/examples/policy-data-class-route/) is such a policy: its settings class a `managed` model `public`, and it halts a build where an assistant holding `restricted` data reaches one with no masking gateway on the route. This is a cross-cutting trait: the same `self-hosted | managed | external` values describe a managed database or a self-run inference server just as they describe a model, so the label lives under the shared `component.aggrega.ai/` namespace rather than the model-specific one.

de47c5b09f6f21ee: **The bundle owns its filenames, and the consuming key owns the directory they land in.** One `artifacts:` entry importing a bundle expands into one output per file in that bundle, each nested under the consumption key as `<key>/<filename>`. The key at the consumption site — `operator-support` above — names the whole consumption rather than any single file; the example emits `operator-support/crd.yaml` and `operator-support/rbac.yaml`. So a bundle name is chosen for legibility at the reference, the filenames are chosen for the reader of the output directory, and neither has to agree with the other. The consumption key is itself bounded to a single filename — a leading letter or digit, then letters, digits, dots, hyphens and underscores, with a key outside that alphabet failing envelope validation — so it names exactly one directory segment, and everything below that segment comes from the bundle. That is what lets a bundle's filenames stay free-form while the key stays strict: a filename is unique within its bundle, a key is unique within its document, and the key is the first segment of every path the entry emits, so no two `artifacts:` entries name one output. Free-form means free within that segment: a filename may carry a nested layout of its own — `crds/widget.yaml` lands at `<key>/crds/widget.yaml` — but it must be an ordinary relative file name beneath the key, written plainly, and a filename that is not one halts the build instead of placing the file somewhere the consuming Recipe never named. That refuses a name climbing above the key or naming an absolute location; `.` or `./`, and a name that collapses back onto the key such as `x/..`, which name the key's own directory rather than a file in it; and a name with a trailing or doubled `/` or a `.` or `..` part — `x/`, `a//b`, `./a`, `a/../b` — which is a second spelling of a file another name can carry, so `a//b` beside `a/b` would put two files at one path. The diagnostic names the bundle file and the key it was imported at. Two outputs that do carry the same filename halt the build when the node renders, which happens when two different input kinds contribute one filename. See [Recipe](recipe.md) for how `artifacts:` composes with the Recipe's other input kinds and for the two non-library authoring modes, and [vocabulary/cross-document-ref](../vocabulary/cross-document-ref.md) for the broader `$ref:` / `$import:` distinction.

It is encapsulated within the Platform Catalog through specialized `components`, `features`, and `recipes`. Developers preserve their specific application intent within their `values` and `uses` blocks — strictly governed by the Architect's `schema:` declarations (compact form or full JSON Schema 2020-12) and `usesSchema` sockets — while the physical translation of that intelligence is executed by target-specific WebAssembly plugins.

advertises, unless `--fetch-trust=false`, `--identity` or `--key` says not to fetch. Under
the offline posture that fetch is refused before anything is dialled, so the registry is

short code `E0310` and names both ways forward: pass `--offline=false` to register it once

baseline, with a notice saying the hub was not asked for its trust policy because the
workspace is offline and the baseline is used instead, and `--fetch-trust=false` registers
the entry from its flags exactly as it does online. The

[`aggrega mcp`](aggrega-mcp.md) behaves the same way: the same refusal in the same words,

e584123fe6ab5bb3: **Topology graph** — renders the selected Release's compiled IR as an interactive graph: boundary and subsystem containers, each boundary or subsystem declared inside another drawn inside it, provenance-styled edges, pan and zoom, click-a-node to select it and double-click to open its source file, and click an edge to select the connection it draws. Each container's title names its kind as well as its grouping, so the outer box and the inner one read apart even in a workspace that declares neither — where both would otherwise carry the same name. A grouping nobody declared, which the compiler creates for components a Release or an Aggregate lists at the top level, is titled as declaring none, and its box is drawn apart from a declared grouping's — a dotted, neutral border — so it does not read as a grouping of that name; one you declared keeps its name whatever it is, `default` included. Each edge carries an arrowhead at the end it points to: an edge runs from the consuming component to its target, and the arrowhead is drawn in the edge's own colour and dash. A node's box is sized by measuring the text it draws, both the node's name and the component beneath it, so neither runs past its border however long the component name is. A legend at the lower left names each grouping by the document that declares it — a boundary by the Release, a subsystem by the Aggregate — and, where the drawing has one, the box holding the nodes in none, with what it holds; it says which end of an edge is its target; and it names the colour bar down a node's leading edge and each colour the drawing gives it, beside the `component.aggrega.ai/type` value that colour stands for exactly as the label is written, with a row for nodes carrying no such label where there are any. It says what those colours do not mean: they are assigned as each graph is drawn, so they group nodes by type within one graph and the same colour in another graph is not the same type. The legend stays where it is whatever you do to the drawing, so wherever the drawing is fitted to the panel — its first drawing, and each time you ask for the graph — it is fitted to the part of the panel above the legend: within the panel's whole width and the height left above the legend, centred from side to side, so the legend covers none of the drawing however many rows it carries. In a panel too short to leave any room above the legend, the drawing is fitted to the whole panel. Selecting a node opens a panel listing what is attached to it: each attachment's Feature and resolved version, the slot it fills or that it fills no declared slot, the FeatureRecipe that realizes it, by name and version, when the compiled graph names one, where it came from, the labels it declares, and the values its author wrote. An attachment written on one of the component's connections — under `features:` on a `uses` entry, in the Aggregate or the Release — is not in that list: it is drawn on the connection it belongs to, as the compiled graph records it, and the node's panel says when its connections carry any. Clicking an edge selects the connection it draws and opens the panel on it, titled by the consuming component and its target and naming the socket and the alias, with that connection's attachments drawn as a node's are — each one's Feature and resolved version, the slot it fills, the FeatureRecipe that realizes it when the compiled graph names one, and its values — or a sentence saying nothing is attached to it. Selecting a node clears a selected connection and the other way round; **Escape** or the panel's close button clears either, and a redraw keeps the selection while the rebuilt graph still draws the node, or the connection from the same component through the same socket under the same alias. Below a node's attachments, under **May attach**, the panel lists the Features whose declared applicability that node's labels satisfy on the graph of the Release the panel shows — the Features declared by the documents in the workspace that Release reads, every one but those in a catalog directory only other Releases read, and those held by the catalog directories that Release builds against — each named with its kind and either the workspace file that declares it or the configured catalog it was resolved from. That list is what those Features declare they apply to, not a decision that attaching one will build — and when it is empty it says that no Feature's declared applicability matches those labels, which is a narrower statement than nothing being attachable. A request the language server could not answer says so in place of the list rather than leaving it blank. A Feature declared behind a link leading out of the workspace — a link to a directory outside it, or a link named like a YAML file that leads to a file outside it — is not offered, because the language server reads no entity through such a link, though your editor's file tree shows the Feature. Where the workspace holds such a link, a line under the list, or under the sentence standing in for an empty one, says so: **Features reached through this link are not offered, because it leads outside the Aggrega workspace:** followed by the link's path relative to the workspace — or **Features reached through these links are not offered, because each leads outside the Aggrega workspace:** for several, the links to directories first. It names the links the language server reports in the terms of the Release the panel shows, as the Catalog panel does in the selected Release's. Where that report cannot be read, the list is drawn without the line and the reason is written to the Aggrega output channel; a list that could not be produced carries no line. Each row carries an **Attach** control that commits it: the compiler is asked which document declares the selected component and where inside that document such an attachment belongs, and the entry is written there through the editor — so it joins the undo history, lands on the buffer you are looking at rather than on the last version saved to disk, and leaves the comments and formatting around it as you wrote them. Nothing is saved on your behalf; the edit is a change like any other, and the compiler re-validates it as it would after any edit. The graph redraws when you save, because the topology is compiled from the documents as they stand on disk and an attachment still sitting in the buffer is not yet part of one. The attachment is named after the Feature, and attaching a Feature already attached under that name is refused rather than written twice. A component declared inside a subsystem attaches by the same press as one declared at the top level, and for the same reason both work: the graph identifies a component by its position in the compiled topology, that position does not say which keys the component's author wrote, and so the extension asks rather than reconstructing — the answer names the document and the path to the block inside it, and both are carried into the edit as they arrived. Where there is no such place to name — an id the graph does not carry, a node it records no document for, or a component whose own block cannot be named in the document it was authored in — what the panel shows is the reason the compiler gave, not a wording of this extension's own. A selected connection's panel has a **May attach** section of its own: the slots that connection's socket declares, in the order the component declares them, each with whether it is required, whether what fills it handles sensitive material, the delivery it permits, its selector and its description, and under each slot the Features the language server answers may fill it on that connection — those whose declared applicability the consuming component's labels satisfy and whose own labels satisfy the slot's selector. Where no slot may be filled, the panel says why in the language server's terms — a Feature drew the connection, the socket is one the component does not declare, or the socket declares no slots — and offers nothing to attach. Pressing **Attach** under a slot writes the Feature under the slot's name, a `<slot>:` entry whose `type:` names the Feature, on that connection's entry in the document that drew the connection: the Release for a connection the Release drew, the Aggregate otherwise. A connection selected from its entry in a document, by **Aggrega: Attach a Feature to the connection at the cursor**, is written in that document instead — the Release, for the Release's own entry for a connection the Aggregate drew — and the panel's line under **May attach** then says the Feature is written on that connection's entry in the document the command was run in. The compiler is asked where that entry goes in that document, any part of the path the document does not carry yet is written with it, and the edit lands in the editor as a node's does, unsaved. A slot the graph already shows filled on that connection is refused before anything is asked, and a refusal from the compiler is shown in its own words. A value the compiler reports as sensitive is withheld by the language server from the graph it sends, and withheld again by the extension before the graph is handed to the view at all, so it is not in the view to be shown — the panel names the field and says why it is withheld, and an attachment whose sensitivity marking is in a shape the panel does not recognise withholds every value rather than guessing at it. An attachment drawn on a connection is withheld by exactly the same rule as one drawn on a node, under the same setting. `aggrega.graph.showSensitiveValues` turns the withholding off for an author who needs to read back what they wrote: only while it is on does the graph request ask the language server for those values, and the settings page says what that displays. Nodes are laid out in deployment-wave order, so a boundary that declares a `syncWave:` appears ahead of the boundaries that wait on it. Hovering a node names its component and resolved version, its labels, its declared wave, and the catalog entity's own metadata — license, repository, home, keywords and maintainers — showing only the fields the entity actually declares. An open graph re-renders itself whenever an authored document in the workspace is saved, so it follows your edits without being reopened; it redraws on a save rather than on a keystroke because the topology is compiled from what is on disk. It redraws as well when the selected Release's lockfile is written — by **Aggrega: Pull**, by a build with Auto pull, or by `aggrega pull` in a terminal — because the graph is pinned against that lockfile, and it also redraws when the language server becomes answerable again, so a graph left open across a restart recovers on its own. A redraw you did not ask for leaves your view where you put it: the pan and zoom you had are kept, whether or not the rebuilt topology differs, so a node the rebuilt layout puts where it was stays under the same part of the panel, and one it puts elsewhere — an added component can shift the ones around it — moves within the view you kept rather than taking the view with it. That includes a redraw that lands while the graph is behind another tab, which you come back to as you left it. **Aggrega: Show topology graph** fits the drawing to the panel again, which is the way back to the whole shape after zooming into part of it. A large topology is fitted whole rather than cropped, so a big one arrives small: you see how it is put together, and reach the names by zooming in. Where two or more groupings held in one box lay out taller than they are wide, they are drawn next to one another rather than stacked in one column, so a large topology uses the panel's width and its first fit draws it larger than a single column would let it. A rebuild the compiler refuses keeps the drawing you had rather than blanking it — the topology is still worth reading and still where you were working — and dims it, so a drawing that is no longer current is not mistaken for one that is; the notice above it carries the compiler's own reason. The drawing comes back to full strength as soon as one is built. Layout is computed in the view; the compiler ships topology, never coordinates.

e60b18d44f52ab2d: **Catalog panel detail** — the entities the workspace can see, grouped under a heading per kind, each row naming the entity and the labels it declares, with its apiVersion and its description in the tooltip. The rows come from two places and each says which. An entity declared by a document in the workspace carries that document's path in its tooltip, and clicking the row opens that file. An entity resolved from a catalog directory — the `catalog/` directory at the workspace root, and the ones your configuration names for the selected Release under `workspace.releases` or, where it names none for it or none is selected, for the whole workspace under `workspace.catalog_dirs` — is marked as coming from there and carries no path: the workspace holds no file of its own for it, so the row names where it came from instead of offering a click with nowhere to go. The list is the selected Release's: a document under a directory your configuration names only for other Releases is left out of it, so where each Release reads a variant of one entity from a directory of its own, the panel lists the selected Release's variant alone. With no Release selected every document in the workspace is listed. A document declaring no `kind:` or no `metadata.name:` is not listed, which is what keeps the panel an index of entities rather than of files. The language server reads no entity through a link leading out of the workspace — a link to a directory outside it, or a link named like a YAML file that leads to a file outside it — so no entity behind one is listed, though your editor's file tree shows it. The one exception is a Release your workspace configuration names, as `build.authoring_release` or as a key of `workspace.releases`, which is read through its link and listed at the link's own place. Where the list leaves such a link out, a row of its own after the list says so: **Entities reached through this link are not listed, because it leads outside the Aggrega workspace:** followed by the link's path relative to the workspace — or **Entities reached through these links are not listed, because each leads outside the Aggrega workspace:** for several, naming the links to directories first and then the links to files. Hovering the row gives the whole sentence, since a long path is cut short in the row. With a Release selected, a link inside a catalog directory only other Releases read is not named, since nothing behind it would be listed for that Release anyway. The list is the language server's own answer, so it names the same entities the compiler reads — unsaved editor buffers included, ahead of the bytes on disk — and it is presented in the order the server sent rather than re-sorted here. The panel reads the list again on its own when the language server becomes answerable, when the selected Release changes, when a `.yaml` document in a folder the window has open is created, changed or deleted on disk — by the editor, a terminal or a checkout alike — and when the editor closes a YAML document. It asks only once the language server has dropped what it held for that file, so a file deleted while it was open in the editor leaves the list rather than being reported from the copy the editor last sent, a document renamed in a buffer and closed without saving is listed again as it stands on disk, and a burst of such changes and closes is one read. The editor closes a document when it lets go of it, which it does not promise to do the moment the document's tab closes, so a row drawn from the text of a document whose tab has closed can stay until the editor does. The panel does not follow your typing on its own. A change still in an unsaved buffer is sent to the language server once you pause typing in that document — each open document waits out its own pause, so typing in one never holds back another — and it shows the next time the list is read after that. Pressing the panel's refresh reads the list for every open document as the editor holds it at the moment you press, however soon after your last keystroke or undo: a change not yet sent is sent at once, and the list is asked for only once the language server has answered for every change sent to it up to the press. A folder deleted whole shows the next time the list is read, or when the refresh is pressed, since the editor may report it as one change to the folder rather than one to each document inside it. Searching the published catalog is this panel's first row, **Search catalog**: it asks for a filter and copies the reference of whatever you pick. Drafting a new entity is its second row, **Draft entity**: it asks for the kind, as a list you pick from, and opens the starter document in a tab without writing anything to disk. This panel's own title bar carries only the refresh. The operations that act on one entity are on that entity's row, and a row offers an operation only where the compiler accepts it for the row's kind. Which kinds each operation accepts is the language server's own answer, read again with the list each time, so the rows follow the compiler you are running rather than a list kept in the extension. Inspecting what an entity resolves to is the one reachable without opening the row's menu: it is addressed by the entity's name, which every row carries, so it is offered on a row whether or not the workspace holds a document for it, wherever the compiler resolves a name to an entity of that kind, and it changes nothing. Validating the entity, checking its publishing conventions and publishing it each take the entity's path, so they are offered only on a row whose entity is declared by a document in this workspace; a row resolved from a configured catalog directory has no path in this workspace to give them, and they are withheld from it rather than offered as controls that could only report a missing argument. Of those three, checking the publishing conventions is offered on every such row. Validating is offered where the compiler checks a document of that kind on its own: an Aggregate, for instance, is checked with the whole catalog when it sits in a catalog directory, and with a Release that deploys it, so its row offers no validation. It checks the entity in the selected Release's terms, as `aggrega validate <path> --release <Release>` does at a terminal, so what the entity refers to — the Component a Recipe implements, a library its schema composes — resolves through the catalog directories that Release builds against; with no Release selected, through the workspace's own. Publishing is offered where a document of that kind is published on its own, which leaves out a Plugin, whose publication also binds its executable, and a Manifest or a Release, neither of which is published. If the language server does not say which operations accept a row's kind, the rows are still listed and a row with a document offers only the conventions check; where the request for that answer fails, its reason is written to the Aggrega output channel. Publishing asks you to confirm first and says what the change reaches: the entity is bundled and pushed under its own declared version, and anyone pulling that version from that registry resolves what is published. Publishing is also the only one of these that changes anything beyond this machine; the two checks and the inspection write nothing and publish nothing. All four show progress and can be stopped.

e84c3e27bb7f5618: **Why every catalog YAML repeats the envelope.** The envelope (`apiVersion`, `kind`, `metadata` block) appears at the top of every catalog file — Component, Feature, Recipe, FeatureRecipe, Aggregate, Manifest, Release, Plugin — regardless of how short the body is. The repetition is deliberate: each file is designed to parse, validate, lint, and inspect as a standalone artefact. A single file pulled from the OCI registry, dropped into a CI sandbox, or opened in a third-party editor must carry enough self-description that downstream tooling can identify what kind of entity it represents and which schema version applies. The directory location never stands in for the envelope: every parser, validator, and linter reads the entity's kind and schema version from the envelope. The cost is mechanical boilerplate per file; the benefit is that the standalone-tooling guarantee holds across the OCI distribution surface, the local filesystem, and the IDE / CI / inspect surfaces. Authors copy the envelope from existing files when authoring new catalog content, or start from `aggrega draft <kind>`, which prints a starter document for the kind with its `apiVersion` and `kind` filled in.

Each fact pairs a name with a value, and both are the guest's own vocabulary: which facts a provider reports, what each name means and what its entries hold are part of that provider's documented contract, not of this socket's. Every fact's value is a list, even when it holds one entry: the host refuses a fact whose value is anything else, naming the provider and the fact, and halts the build. That is the one thing the host learns about a value. It keys facts by name and hands each list to the templates that read it, joining the lists of one name reported by more than one render of the same node in the order those renders ran, and it never learns what a name or an entry means or derives a fact itself — so a provider can report something only its own format knowledge can see, such as a property of the documents it wrote, without the host learning that format. Reporting facts never changes what is written: the files the host writes are the files the guest returned, whether or not facts accompany them. The guest lists its facts in a fixed order so the payload is byte-identical across runs of identical input. Each entry is itself a Go template, evaluated against a self-contained context: '.context.instance_id' (the HOST COMPONENT this attachment is resolving for, which is what that reference denotes on every template surface), '.attachment_name' (the attachment instance being resolved, and the only route to that name from a local), the attachment's own '.values' and '.infra', and the entries of this same block resolved so far. Entries resolve in the order they are written, and an entry MAY read a sibling defined ABOVE it, receiving that sibling's resolved value rather than its template text. Author order is part of the contract wherever one entry reads another: moving a definition below its reader breaks the build, and the block is never reordered to make a reference resolve. A '.locals.<key>' reference to an entry this block defines LATER halts naming the ordering fault; one naming a key the block does not declare at all halts naming the key. Both checks read the path a reference RESOLVES to rather than the keystrokes, so they cover the direct form, a read inside a '{{ with .locals }}' block, and a read through a variable bound directly to '.locals' alike. Two spellings they do not cover. One is a reference whose path the template text does not decide — one reached through a function, such as 'index .locals', or through a 'with' block or a variable binding whose pipeline applies one, since what such a pipeline yields is decided at evaluation rather than by its text. The other is a key read off a parenthesised block, '(.locals).<key>' or '($.locals).<key>', where the key hangs off the value the parentheses yield rather than off the block itself. Neither is analysed, and an absent key reached either way does not halt: it renders the literal text '<no value>' rather than nothing at all. The one exception is 'index' itself: on every template surface it halts, naming the key, when the map it reads does not hold the key it is asked for, so an absent key reached through 'index .locals' halts. This FeatureRecipe's locals resolve BEFORE its provides, so a provides template may read '.locals' and receives resolved values, while a provides template naming a key this block does not declare halts. The rendered values differ across environments while the Aggregate — the authoring surface for *which* values exist and *how* they flow — remains the single source of truth. Crucially, to prevent untraceable "aggregate-mutating" Releases, when a Release uses `extends`, declaring an `aggregate` is rejected by the Release schema (the schema constraint disallows declaring `aggregate` when `extends` is used). ed4dec9759b91cb6: Map of entry name to artifact-content authoring. Each entry's value carries one of three modes via content-shape dispatch. Mode 1 (inline): a Go template string scalar whose output is the artifact body. Mode 2 (file import): a YAML map of exactly one key, `$import: ./relative/path.yaml`, pointing at a local Go-template file. Mode 3 (library import): a YAML map of exactly one key, `$import: <Library>#/artifacts/<entry>`, referencing an ArtifactLibrary bundle by bare-name identity (the version is supplied by the per-Release lockfile; no registry host appears in the reference). A bundle expands into one output per file, each nested under the entry's key as `<key>/<filename>`. The key names the entry's output: a mode-1 or mode-2 entry's key is its output filename, used as written, and a mode-2 entry's imported file supplies the content without naming the output, so two entries importing different files that share a name are two distinct outputs. The auxiliary resources a resource-generating FeatureRecipe emits (ConfigMap, ServiceMonitor, NetworkPolicy, ExternalSecret CRD, etc.) are artifact-shaped; artifacts: is the primary resource-generation mechanism. Collisions across artifact entries, bundle files, source output, and workload synthesis halt the build when the node renders. The `artifacts` block is authored identically on a Recipe and on a FeatureRecipe — the same three modes, the same key-to-output rule and the same collision behaviour — which is why that part of this description reads the same on both kinds; an example written for one transfers to the other unchanged. In the object form, `$import` must not match `^oci://`; a value that does is rejected. Keys: The key names the entry's output, so it is bounded to a single filename: it begins with a letter or digit and continues with letters, digits, dots, hyphens or underscores. Dots after the first character keep the extensions artifact keys carry (`main.tf`, `template.yaml`, `serviceaccount.yaml`). A `/` would make one key name a path rather than a file, and a leading `.` would admit `..`, which names a location outside the output directory — the first character class refuses both. For a library import the key names the directory the bundle's files are nested under, so the same bound applies. Pattern: `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*$`.

**Only the router's own routes are reachable.** The guard sees only the routes
that hand it the request, so the second ConfigMap's other file configures the
pod's second container, which mounts that ConfigMap alone and runs the official
nginx image as a path allowlist. The router itself listens on the pod's
loopback address, where nothing outside the pod reaches it, and the allowlist
listens on port 4000, the port the Service below targets. It forwards a request
only when its method and path are one of the routes the router serves — the
model request routes the guard checks, in the spellings the router serves
whatever the alias, `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/messages` among them; the
model listing; the health checks; and, of its
administrative routes, key management — and answers every other path 403,
forwarding nothing. So the proxy's token-count routes, its pass-through routes to
providers' own APIs, its other administrative routes and its administrative
console cannot be reached through the router, and neither can a model route
whose path carries the model name, as the paths Azure's client sends do:
there the proxy reads words in the path, the alias included, to decide how it
records a request, and the router would refuse a request for this map's own
`assistant` on it. The proxy's metrics are not among those routes either: port
4000 answers `/metrics` 403. With the router's `metrics_enabled` true, as the
Aggregate sets it, the allowlist also listens on port 9090 and forwards a GET of
`/metrics` there alone, to the listener the proxy keeps for its metrics on the
loopback address, answering every other request 403. That port checks no
caller, and the metrics name the hashed keys, key aliases and user emails the
router attributes spend to.
