Their importers read only those declarations — a CrewAI project's agent and task files, a LangGraph application's `langgraph.json`, a Google ADK application's agent configurations, an Agent Framework declarative agent — and draft the standard library's agent for the framework around a program they never open, wired to what the declarations name: the model an agent asks for, the datastore a LangGraph checkpointer keeps state in, the MCP servers an Agent Framework agent reaches. The program runs in the image the Release names. What only the program says — the logic of a task, a tool its code defines, an agent its code builds — is named in the draft's comments and decisions and becomes no Component; carrying it into authoring files is the author's work, by hand or with an AI assistant authoring on the author's behalf through [`aggrega mcp`](../authoring/getting-started.md#authoring-with-an-ai-assistant), which reads the reference and scaffolds and validates entities.
efe125bdc1ec5dfb: **Kong in front of models:** `core/gateway/kong`, the open-source Kong gateway, serves the models wired to its own `models` socket through Kong's AI proxy, and of the controls below it realizes prompt deny patterns alone, as Kong's AI Prompt Guard on every route of each wired model. Each wired model gets a chat route and a completion route under `/<alias>/v1`, written from the `endpoint` and `model` the model publishes, and its Recipes import those routes into the gateway's PostgreSQL backend before it starts. The route chooses the model, so a request is sent to the model its path names whatever model name it carries. The gateway presents each connection's own credential as a bearer token its configuration reads from the gateway's environment by name, and a connection reaching a model whose `model.aggrega.ai/api` is not `openai` halts the build. It publishes the route of the alias its `values.model` names as its `endpoint` and that alias as its `model`, and carries `model.aggrega.ai/api: openai`, so an agent's `model` socket takes it as it takes the AI gateway. With nothing wired to that socket the gateway serves no model and publishes both keys empty, and an agent wired to it then reads no address and no model name. The import adds and updates routes and removes none, so a route whose connection is removed keeps answering, and the prompt guard a `core/prompt-deny-patterns` attachment wrote keeps refusing once the attachment is removed, until each is deleted through Kong's Admin API. For the same reason the gateway declares no callers, and its model routes check no caller's key: Kong tells callers apart only as the consumers an authentication plugin names, and a consumer and its key, once imported, would stay able to authenticate after the caller is removed from the Release, a rotated key leaving the old one working; nor can a key-auth key be held by reference, so a caller's key could reach Kong only as a literal in a rendered file.

f2e0f35a55e2f496: `core/secret-value` has a second Helm realization, **`k8s-secret-from-value`**, for a consumer that reads its credential by reference rather than off the inject pipe: the synthesized `helm/postgres`, for one, renders its `password` slot as a `secretKeyRef`, which a fill publishing no locator cannot satisfy. It writes the value into a Kubernetes Secret it emits from a co-located chart, the `k8s-secret-from-parameter` shape above, publishes that Secret's `name` and `key` as `provides`, and also delivers the value into the inject pipe exactly as `env-secret` does, so a Recipe reading the pipe receives it as a variable. One Manifest mapping therefore serves consumers of both kinds, and the same `core/secret-value` attachments build for Compose and for Helm — except an `origin` written as a Compose variable reference such as `${DB_PASSWORD}`, which nothing on the Helm path substitutes: `env-secret` and `k8s-secret-from-value` both refuse it at build time, so set the real value through the Release, as a parameter the Aggregate hoists into the origin or as `infra.origin` in place of the origin the Aggregate writes. The value sits in the rendered output either way — in the Secret, and in the manifest of a consumer reading the pipe. Reach for `env-secret` where every consumer reads the pipe and no Secret is wanted, for `k8s-secret-from-value` where one reads by reference, and for `core/referenced-secret` bound to `k8s-existing-secret` or `k8s-external-secret` where the credential must stay out of the rendered output.

**`ir-verdict`** — the guest reasons over the intermediate-representation
  graph, before rendering. The payload carries the full capability-agnostic IR graph (every
  node, edge, and attachment the compiler holds) plus the routing paths the
  analyzer enumerates, so a policy can reason about topology and reachability
  without re-walking the graph. That path list is **bounded per starting node** —
  a densely connected or cyclic topology can hold more distinct routes than the
  enumeration emits, and once the bound is reached the remaining routes from that
  starting node are not listed. A path that is present is therefore real, while
  the absence of a path is not proof that none exists: a policy whose verdict
  turns on something being *unreachable* should establish that from the nodes and
  edges, which the payload carries in full, rather than from the path list alone.
  One thing in the graph is not as written: every value an author declared
  sensitive — in an attachment's `values` or `infra`, in a boundary
  attachment's `infra`, or in a node's own `values` or `infra` — arrives as the
  withheld marker `{"aggrega_withheld": "declared"}`, while its key, its
  sensitivity marking and every undeclared value beside it arrive as written. A
  policy judges where declared-sensitive material travels and never receives the
  material; see
  [the attachment facts a governance policy reads](governance-attachment-facts.md#declared-sensitive-values-arrive-withheld).
  An `ir-verdict` policy runs at the static-analysis
  gate, before any artifacts are produced. Use it for policies about
  architecture and wiring — topology invariants, cross-boundary auth,
  credential-flow shape — that should halt a build before it renders anything.

f509e371715df0db: **The plugin whose rules are read is the one serving the capability in your workspace when you pin**: your workspace's provider binding for that capability, or else the plugin built into `aggrega`. The step records that plugin — its reference and the digest of its entity — and the exact rules it composed in the `entity.lock`. From then on, every reading of the directory applies the recorded rules and no others: a publication of the entity, the comparison a pull or a push holds the lock to, the entity's row in a lockfile, a build's comparison, the render that hands the directory to a provider, and `aggrega pull --verify`. So what you publish is exactly what your own build renders, and a changed binding, an edited `.aggregaignore` or a newer `aggrega` changes nothing until you pin again — at which point the lock's diff shows what moved. A file a plugin names as an ignore file, such as a `.helmignore`, is itself one of the source's files and is pinned like any other unless a rule leaves it out, so editing it without pinning again is caught by the next pull or build. f665dd49c4fc48db: The Private Ops State. Internal computation results available within this Recipe's templates as '.locals.*'. Each entry is itself a Go template, evaluated against a self-contained node-local context: '.context.instance_id', '.values', '.infra', and the entries of this same block resolved so far. Entries resolve in the order they are written, and an entry MAY read a sibling defined ABOVE it, receiving that sibling's resolved value rather than its template text. Author order is part of the contract wherever one entry reads another: moving a definition below its reader breaks the build, and the block is never reordered to make a reference resolve. A '.locals.<key>' reference to an entry this block defines LATER halts naming the ordering fault; one naming a key the block does not declare at all halts naming the key. Both checks read the path a reference RESOLVES to rather than the keystrokes, so they cover the direct form, a read inside a '{{ with .locals }}' block, and a read through a variable bound directly to '.locals' alike. Two spellings they do not cover. One is a reference whose path the template text does not decide — one reached through a function, such as 'index .locals', or through a 'with' block or a variable binding whose pipeline applies one, since what such a pipeline yields is decided at evaluation rather than by its text. The other is a key read off a parenthesised block, '(.locals).<key>' or '($.locals).<key>', where the key hangs off the value the parentheses yield rather than off the block itself. Neither is analysed, and an absent key reached either way does not halt: it renders the literal text '<no value>' rather than nothing at all. The one exception is 'index' itself: on every template surface it halts, naming the key, when the map it reads does not hold the key it is asked for, so an absent key reached through 'index .locals' halts. A local cannot read '.provides': that pillar is not part of this context, and an entry reaching for it halts. The resolved values reach provides, source, valuesMapping, workload, artifacts, assertions, and pipeline[].with (and pipeline[].when) — this Recipe's locals resolve BEFORE its provides, so a provides template may read '.locals' and receives resolved values, while a provides template naming a key this block does not declare halts. Used to export physical realities (e.g., target containers, JSON paths) for downstream Wasm plugins. Never exposed to callers — use provides for the public API.

Accepting `JWT` does mean the declared type alone no longer tells an access token from an identity token — the audience check is what tells them apart, and it is why that check is the load-bearing one: an identity token's audience is the client it was issued to, never this deployment's own `mcp.authorization.resource`, so a token issued for anything but this deployment is refused whatever it calls itself.

f894fadba3e3977f: The wire shapes a Provider render plugin socket consumes and emits. A Provider guest renders one IR node into output files on its render_node export (RenderNodeInput to RenderNodeOutput), and optionally merges the per-node outputs at one boundary into a single assembled artifact on its assemble_boundary export (AssembleBoundaryInput to AssembleBoundaryOutput). AssembleBoundaryOutput carries the assembled files and any diagnostics; where each contributor's files sit is declared once on the guest's describe() contract rather than on this reply. A guest may also declare an optional validate_node_input export that structurally checks a node's resolved input before render dispatch: it consumes the same RenderNodeInput projection render_node receives and returns a ValidateNodeOutput carrying only diagnostics — a halt-severity diagnostic stops the build loudly, a warn-severity diagnostic surfaces to the build result. A guest whose target bounds or restricts the names it accepts may also declare an optional name_bound export, which the host asks before it settles a node's component identity: it consumes a NameBoundInput carrying one proposed name and returns a NameBoundOutput carrying one verdict per kind of name the guest would derive from it. A verdict carries a constraint — usable, or bounded to a shorter length — and never a name the guest built, so the knowledge of what the target accepts stays in the guest. Separately, a guest whose target derives a name of its own for the resources it renders — from author-supplied source, or from a workload it synthesizes — may declare an optional rendered_name export, which the host asks so a Recipe author can read that name and publish an address built from it: it consumes a RenderedNameInput carrying the identities the target derives from and the input kinds the node's Recipe declares, and returns a RenderedNameOutput carrying the name the guest itself will render under, or no name where it derives none. The two exports are opposite directions of one subject and neither stands in for the other — name_bound asks the guest to judge a name the host proposes, while rendered_name reports a name the guest composed, which the host carries without reading. The guest returns each output file's serialized bytes; the host writes them verbatim and runs no serializer, so determinism is the guest's responsibility: identical input must produce identical bytes. The wire shapes are co-canonical with the host's Go render types and with each per-language plugin-development-kit mirror; cross-language round-trip tests catch drift.

f8bdd78fc364a446: `aggrega/resolveDependencies` — resolve the Release's catalog and source dependencies into the cache, pin the external inputs its render consumes into the content-addressed store, and write its lockfile. `release` is a path relative to the workspace root, the same value `aggrega/irGraph` takes and refused in the same shapes. `upgrade` discards the recorded pins and re-resolves, floating each dependency to the highest available version; `targets` narrows that to the entity references it names, holding every other pin. `verify` checks the recorded resolution against the one this request would perform without it, honouring the recorded pins the same way, and writes no lockfile, [plugin trust record](aggrega-pull.md#the-plugin-trust-record) or `entity.lock` — the cache is read and filled as it would be without it — answering `verified: true` and the `toolchain` the lockfile records. `verify` is refused as invalid params beside `upgrade`, beside `targets`, and beside `pinSources` whichever value it carries, before anything is resolved or any progress is reported: an upgrade drops the pins a verify exists to honour, named targets are re-resolved only by an upgrade, and `pinSources` decides whether a resolution records the pins an `entity.lock` is missing or refuses over them, neither of which a comparison that writes no `entity.lock` does. The command line and the assistant tool refuse the same pairs. The answer names the `lockfile` it wrote or compared against and every reference it pinned, in `entities`, `libraries` and `plugins`, each entry carrying the `version` it resolved to and its `source` — where this run took the reference from, in the word [`aggrega pull --detail`](aggrega-pull.md#the-lockfile) prints for the same resolution: `fetched-fresh`, `cache-reuse`, `local`, `in-binary` or `external` — alongside `sourceArtifacts`, `trustedPlugins`, `externalInputs` — how many external inputs the lockfile pins once the run is done, counting both the ones carried forward and the ones this run discovered — and any `notices` the resolution raised. 🔴 **A successful answer does not by itself mean the external-input pinning is complete.** Where the run pinned every dependency but could not finish working out which external inputs the Release consumes, it answers `incompleteExternalInputs` saying what stopped the discovery, and it still answers as a success — the dependency pins are complete and on disk, so reporting the whole request as failed would tell you to redo work that is already correct. **Read that field before treating a lockfile as fully pinned:** it is absent when nothing was left undiscovered, so its presence is the signal. There is no catalog-directory parameter: the search stack is the one the workspace configures. **This is the session's one pinning request for a Release, and it is where external inputs are pinned too** — which URLs a render consumes follows from what it renders, so this request renders the Release to find out, and a build request is then served from what it recorded. A Recipe or FeatureRecipe the Release builds whose `entity.lock` records no pin for an input the entity reads refuses the request, naming `aggrega pin` and each input left unrecorded; `pinSources: true` runs that pin step over those entities instead, writing the `entity.lock` beside each — the same step `aggrega/pin` runs, writing the same bytes. Absent, `pinSources` follows the workspace's `pin_sources_at_pull`; sent, it overrides that setting in both directions, so `false` refuses even in a workspace configured to pin. This request reaches registries and writes — see [Reaching a registry, and writing](#reaching-a-registry-and-writing).

f9cc6029258d9be8: **Composite Aggregates are SUPPORTED (The Module Pattern):** Aggregates act as both the root Aggregate a Release builds and reusable modules. A parent Aggregate can declare a child Aggregate exactly like a component, passing `parameters` down into it. To prevent tight coupling, child Aggregates expose an **`exportedComponents:`** contract, establishing a stable public interface name. The parent reaches the module's components only through this interface: a `uses:` target names the module and one of its exported aliases, and the compiler wires the edge to the internal component the alias names, while a target that reaches into a module by any other name halts the build, naming the module and the aliases it exports. A target that resolves to no internal node still halts loudly, and a re-export chain that closes back on itself is rejected rather than followed forever.

The message names the key either way, which is what keeps the report equally actionable — but where in the message to read it differs across the four forms above, so read the field path for the block and then take the key from whichever of the four you have: where the detail leads with the delivery mechanism, the key is the quoted value straight after it; where the detail leads with the key on its own, it is the first quoted value; and where the detail leads with the delivery entry's own path, the key is that path's last step.
